articles.title: Shau Kei Wan water supply returns after pipe burst
articles.excerpt: The government said emergency repair works conducted after a water pipe burst in Shau Kei Wan have been completed, with…
articles.fullText:
The government said emergency repair works conducted after a water pipe burst in Shau Kei Wan have been completed, with fresh water supply to users in the area returning to normal from 9.30pm on Tuesday.

In a social media post, the Water Supplies Department said that because the incident involved a large and complex system of pipes, people living at the ends of the water supply network or at higher elevations may need to wait up to three to four hours before the water reaches them.

The department said it would continue to provide water trucks and tanks until the fresh water supply fully returns to normal.

It also said it is normal for the water to appear milky or slightly turbid upon supply restoration.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Boeing delays 737 production target to early 2027
articles.excerpt: Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said on Tuesday that the company will not reach its 737 production rate target of 47…
articles.fullText:
Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said on Tuesday that the company will not reach its 737 production rate target of 47 jets a month until next year, a serious setback to the company's ongoing recovery.

The company had planned to reach the target this past summer, but it will take "into early next year," Ortberg said during an interview on CNBC.

In September, he said that Boeing has not been able to make wings fast enough.

Deliveries of the popular single-aisle jetliner are a major driver of Boeing's cash flow.

Shares of the US planemaker fell 2.5 percent in premarket trading even as Boeing continues to recover from years of crises and controversies that dented its reputation, drained cash and saddled it with a heavy debt load.

During the quarter, Boeing secured certification for the 737 MAX 7 from US regulators, won the US Navy's sixth-generation F/A-XX fighter contract and generated free cash flow for another quarter, while certification of the larger MAX 10 followed in October.

"Expectations are rising, and they should. We have a stronger foundation than a year ago, but we also have more work to do to deliver on our backlog, strengthen our culture, and improve how we work every day," Ortberg said in a memo to employees after the results.

Boeing reported an adjusted loss of 34 cents per share for the quarter through September, compared with market expectation of 21 cents, according to data compiled by LSEG.

Revenue at Boeing Commercial Airplanes dipped slightly to US$10.7 billion, while operating loss stood at US$697 million and margin shrank by just 6.5 percent compared with a contraction of 48.3 percent a year ago.

The company attributed the performance to less profitable jetliner deliveries and higher production costs, including from its supply chain.

At Boeing's defense division, higher deliveries, improved operational performance and a US$252-million sale of a subsidiary contributed to nearly US$500 million in quarterly earnings with an operating margin of 6.2 percent, up from 1.7 percent a year ago.

Boeing Global Services earned US$1 billion and posted an operating margin of 18.3 percent.

The US planemaker ended the quarter with US$25.2 billion in net debt, down slightly from US$25.9 billion in the previous three months and US$30.4 billion a year ago. (Reuters)

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Qatar, Iran leader discussed war in Moscow meeting
articles.excerpt: Qatar's ruler and the Iranian president discussed the Middle East war and the blockaded Strait of Hormuz during a meeting…
articles.fullText:
Qatar's ruler and the Iranian president discussed the Middle East war and the blockaded Strait of Hormuz during a meeting in Moscow, the emir's office said on Tuesday.

The high-level meeting came a day after senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan held talks with Iran in Tehran in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting.

Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met on Tuesday on the sidelines of a summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum in Moscow.

Pezeshkian is also due to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin later in the day.

The Qatari and Iranian leaders "reviewed the current state of relations between Tehran and Doha and emphasised the importance of deepening political and economic ties and making use of existing potential to strengthen bilateral cooperation," Iranian state television said.

Qatar and Pakistan have been at the forefront of efforts to secure a lasting deal between the United States and Iran.

On Sunday, a Qatari delegation visited Tehran and "reviewed developments in the regional situation, foremost among them the latest on the negotiations, the Strait of Hormuz, and energy supplies", Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said earlier.

On Tuesday, Qatari foreign ministry official Ibrahim Al-Hashmi said the region needed a new security framework to prevent further violence.

"The ball is now in Iran's court to commit to these principles and demonstrate good faith," he said.

"We have heard positive statements from the Iranian side... but they still need to demonstrate good faith, stop threatening countries of the region, and reopen the Strait of Hormuz so that all those efforts can go towards having a safe and prosperous region," he added.

Monday's talks in Tehran included Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan's army chief General Asim Munir and Turkiye's intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin. Iran described them as "very good".

They followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war, which saw Tehran strike US allies in the region including Qatar.

In early October, Putin said Russia was prepared to take part in mediation to bring an end to the war. (AFP)

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: The Download: Anthropic’s IPO, smarter power grids, and exercise pills
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Will the real Anthropic please stand up?

After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and how it believes it will change the world.

But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture, presenting it as different things to different people: an AI safety organization, a profit-driven megacorp, and a group hell-bent on creating superhuman technology.

These roles come with huge tensions. Will the IPO reveal the company behind the mask, or lean deeper into the myth-making? Take a new glimpse inside Anthropic .

—Will Douglas Heaven

This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.

How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom

Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping efficiently move power across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.

As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses.

The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.

Find out how solid-state transformers could help meet rising electricity demand .

—Casey Crownhart

Are we there yet? Exercise in a pill

We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks, without the workout.

The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.

Discover how close researchers are to developing an exercise pill .

—Cassandra Willyard

This story is part of “Are we there yet?” from the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review . The series takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Over the next six days, we’ll explore each one in The Download.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Anthropic has filed for its blockbuster IPO
The listing could determine the future of the AI investment boom. ( CNBC )
+ The filing warns of catastrophic AI risks and huge compute costs. ( BBC )
+ And exposes safety failures and a month-long training pause. ( Reuters $)
+ The prospectus reveals soaring revenues but also staggering losses. ( NYT $)
+ Anthropic’s founders will retain voting control after the IPO. ( Verge ) 

2 Solar is quietly overtaking nuclear as a global power source
Cheap panels and batteries are accelerating the shift. ( BBC )
+ The balcony solar boom is coming to the US. ( MIT Technology Review )

3 OpenAI has announced three new science discoveries
They span mathematics, computer science, and physics. ( Verge )
+ It’s enlisted expert “shepherds” to publish its breakthroughs. ( Gizmodo )

4 Microsoft is offering buyouts to a quarter of staff amid rising AI costs
Around 60,000 employees are eligible for the buyout program. ( Bloomberg $)
+ Microsoft plans $190 billion in AI spending this year. ( NYT $)

5 The plastics industry knew microplastics could enter the body decades ago
Company documents reveal concerns dating back to 1974. ( LA Times $)
+ No part of the globe is free of human fingerprints. ( MIT Technology Review )

6 A demonstration of lighting Earth from space has sparked alarm
Startup Reflect Orbital used space mirrors for the California test. ( Guardian )
+ The tech could jeopardize the night sky. ( MIT Technology Review )

7 The US has designated helium a critical material
The move is due to its importance to semiconductor production. ( AP )

8 Hundreds of Boston Dynamics staff have protested its ICE deal
They’ve called for a halt to sales of the robot dogs. ( Ars Technica )

9 Treatments for age-related infertility are being developed at last
Two startups aim to reduce chromosome errors in eggs. ( Economist $)
+ Here’s how tech transformed babymaking. ( MIT Technology Review )

10 Grok says its AI-generated Odyssey is “not historically accurate”
The bot itself admitted Elon Musk’s filmmaking plan has failed. ( Wired $)

Quote of the day

“It’s as if they’re making a promise and crossing their fingers behind their backs.”

—Kate Brennan, who leads policy at the AI Now Institute, tells the New York Times that the voluntary safety pledges AI executives recently made are toothless and unenforceable.

One more thing

MCKIBILLO

The problem with thinking you’re part Neanderthal

There’s a theory that many of us have an “inner Neanderthal.” The idea is that Homo sapiens and its cousin species once bred, leaving some people today with a trace of Neanderthal DNA.

This DNA is arguably the 21st century’s most celebrated discovery in human evolution. But in 2024, a pair of French geneticists called into question the theory’s very foundations.

They proposed that what scientists interpret as interbreeding could instead be explained by population structure—the way genes concentrate in smaller, isolated groups.

Find out what it all means for human evolution .

—Ben Crair

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ See how fast the planets spin with this dizzying animation that puts faces on each one.
+ A flask of mercury, a little neon, and some shaking produce this mesmerizing homemade light .
+ What can the USA’s earliest restaurants teach us about the country? This digital collection explores the answers.
+ Rick and Morty asked the crucial question: could a lightsaber really drill its way to Earth’s core? Science now has an answer .

articles.title: Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
articles.excerpt: Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence. Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers. Consider…
articles.fullText:
Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence. Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers.

Consider an experienced operator preparing to restart a line after a changeover. The machine settings matter, but so does knowing how a particular material behaves, what happened during the previous shift, and when an apparently minor variation deserves a closer look. A procedure can describe the sequence, but successful execution depends on the judgment that comes from experience and the organization’s accumulated know-how.

That combination is industrial intelligence: a manufacturer’s accumulated know-how, operating practices, production data, and understanding of its own business.

The opportunity now is to make more of that intelligence available wherever decisions are made, then connect it to the physical world of manufacturing. The strategic destination is not more agents, but rather to turn the existing business intelligence into an engine for profitable growth.

Individual knowledge can be translated into organizational advantage

Expertise has limited reach when it stays with one person, inside one system, or within one plant. Leaders now must determine how to extend that reach without stripping away the context that makes the knowledge useful.

For example, an engineer evaluating a process change needs more than a production record. They need to understand the circumstances behind it: the equipment configuration, the quality requirements, and the trade-offs an operator made. Connecting those elements can help people apply experience beyond the place where it originated.

When individual knowledge becomes widely accessible, innovation can spread to the maintenance workshop, the planning office, the engineering team, and the production floor. More people can contribute because more people can work with what the organization knows.

But access to knowledge is only part of the opportunity. Manufacturing ultimately is physical, and it depends on materials, machines, and products.

When intelligence participates in action

Physical AI describes systems that can perceive conditions, reason about them, and take action within the physical world. By connecting machines and processes, manufacturers get a clearer view of what is happening on the factory floor. Agents can then reason on top of that information to identify patterns, predict problems, and determine the best course of action. Physical AI brings business intelligence into the physical process, allowing machines and systems to respond to changing conditions.

Consider a robotic-handling operation encountering variation in the parts arriving at its station. Vision can help the system assess a part’s position. A model informed by the material and task can help determine an appropriate movement. Connected controls can then execute an adjustment within validated limits. The value is not merely seeing the variation; it is responding appropriately.

The same principle applies to quality operations. When Toyota Industries connected previously fragmented paint shop data, engineering and operations teams were given the context needed to understand defect drivers. The company reports that analysis cycles fell from five days to under four hours, while its pilot reduced relevant paint defects by about 25%. The breakthrough was not simply identifying another signal; it was helping people understand why defects were occurring and respond before the outcome was locked in.

This is the type of situation where industrial intelligence has become essential. Data may reveal what is happening, but industrial intelligence provides the context for what should happen, which constraints cannot be breached, and when uncertainty requires human judgment.

Simulation offers a way to examine proposed actions before applying them to equipment. Manufacturers can explore how a change might affect a process in a digital environment. That does not remove the need for physical validation, but it creates room to learn without treating the production line as the first experiment.

Responsible deployment, therefore, begins with operational discipline. Leaders need to establish clear authority or what systems may change, reliable connections to equipment, defined safety boundaries, and a record of decisions and actions. People must be able to recognize uncertainty, intervene, and bring equipment to a safe state. Trust rests on those practical arrangements, not on confidence in a model alone.

More capable machines, more capable people

Manufacturing has long combined human ingenuity with increasingly capable tools. Physical AI extends that relationship. Intelligent equipment can take on suitable repetitive or physically demanding tasks, while agent-assisted operations can help people navigate information-intensive decisions and changing conditions.

The aim is not to make machines smarter; it is to see what people can build when knowledge can travel, intelligence can act, and ambition has more room to become reality.

Rockwell Automation illustrates the point. At its Singapore plant, technicians use a maintenance copilot that combines manufacturing data, machine manuals, and knowledge captured from experienced workers. This system has reduced the time required for new workers to learn how to troubleshoot hundreds of machines from nine months to three. An engineer could explore more process alternatives before committing to a change. An operator could help improve the system’s response rather than repeatedly managing the same exception.

This type of progress requires investment in equipment but also in people: training, time to learn, and playing a meaningful role in shaping how systems work. Machines become more capable so people can become more capable.

Industrial Intelligence is the answer to sustainable growth

Industrial intelligence connects what a manufacturer knows: the experience of its people, the signals from its operations, and the lessons accumulated over time. Physical AI gives that intelligence a way to act in the physical world, turning knowledge into decisions and decisions into action.

The next challenge for industry is not simply to produce more, but to grow without adding complexity at the same rate. Intelligence can help manufacturers turn experience into scalable capability—improving productivity, accelerating innovation, expanding capacity, and enabling people to solve problems that were previously difficult to tackle.

The next frontier of industry is not smarter machines or more automated factories; it is businesses that can continuously learn, adapt, and act. The opportunity is to turn the intelligence embedded in every operation into a compounding advantage for growth.

Watch the video series to learn how industrial customers are unlocking intelligence across the value chain, and join Microsoft at Microsoft Ignite to see what’s next for Industrial Intelligence.

This content was produced by Microsoft. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

articles.title: Hung Hom skybridge 'to serve as viewing platform'
articles.excerpt: The Development Bureau said on Tuesday a skybridge between two buildings to be constructed on Hung Hom waterfront would also…
articles.fullText:
The Development Bureau said on Tuesday a skybridge between two buildings to be constructed on Hung Hom waterfront would also serve as a viewing platform and a venue for public activities.

The plan was revealed as the bureau revised its development proposal for sites around Hung Hom MTR station and the district's harbourfront areas following a public consultation.

Permanent Secretary for Development Doris Ho told lawmakers the authorities plan to connect two mixed-use towers proposed to be constructed at the waterfront area.

The skybridge connecting the buildings would create an open space that could serve as a viewing platform, she said at a meeting of the Legislative Council’s development panel.

“Our current plan is that the space will be open to the public. But whether it will operate on a commercial basis or be open for free is something we need to keep flexible and decide at the next stage,” Ho said.

“Apart from allowing people to enjoy views of Victoria Harbour, we also have an idea that this space could be opened up for holding events.”

According to a document submitted to the legislature, the entire development at Hung Hom is expected to provide more than 200,000 square metres of gross floor area – an increase by three percent compared with the previous plan.

This includes more than 60 percent of areas for residential use and over 30 percent for commercial purposes.

Ho said the bureau had adjusted the allocation of floor space by cutting the floor area for commercial use and increasing the residential areas amid lower demand for the former.

Edited by Edmond Fong

Mainland stocks gave up gains earlier in the day to close at a 14-month low on Tuesday, with tech shares resuming their decline after a brief rise on an uptick in sentiment in the region.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index fell 170 points, or 0.7 percent, to 23,041 on turnover of HK$178.35 billion.

The tech index was down 57 points, or 1.5 percent, at 3,800 while the China enterprises index slipped 35 points, or 0.5 percent, to 7,766.

Up north, the Shanghai Composite Index closed down 49 points, or 1.33 percent, at 3,648 on turnover of 672.4 billion yuan while the blue-chip CSI300 Index was also 1.3 percent lower.

The Shenzhen Component Index fell 288 points, or 2.5 percent, to close at 11,245 on turnover of 788.5 billion yuan while the ChiNext Index dived 90 points, or 3.41 percent, to 2,548 on turnover of 381.58 billion yuan.

Shanghai's tech-focused Star50 index slumped 4.8 percent to the lowest since March.

The selloff in Chinese AI-related shares, however, continued, with the CSI Semiconductor Index down 5.8 percent at a fresh six-month low and the CSI AI Index down nearly four percent.

"The market may stage a short-term rebound after the recent selloff, but a more sustained recovery could require further de-leveraging over the medium term as some crowded positions have yet to be fully cleared," analysts at Sinolink Securities said in a note.

China's central bank said on Monday it had decided to establish a swap facility to provide emergency liquidity to non-bank financial institutions facing large-scale redemptions.

"The establishment of such facilities to address large redemptions at non-bank financial institutions could keep short-term liquidity conditions accommodative," Huajin Securities analysts said in a note.

Elsewhere, data released on Tuesday showed China's industrial profits grew at a faster pace in September, but the sectoral divide remained pronounced.

Around the region, Asian stocks climbed as AI firm Anthropic's eagerly anticipated IPO filing lifted risk appetite ahead of tech earnings that will be a test for the AI trade, and central bank meetings that will influence near-term interest rates.

In Tokyo, the tech-heavy Nikkei share average rebounded 1,078 points, or 1.73 percent, to close the day at 63,268 after paring an earlier gain of more than two percent.

The broader Topix rose 24 points, or 0.61 percent, to 3,997.

In Seoul, the Kospi closed up 168 points, or 3.09 percent, at 5,638 after rising up to 4.9 percent during the session.

articles.title: Polls open in Israel as Netanyahu battles for survival
articles.excerpt: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a fight for political survival on Tuesday in an election seen by many Israelis…
articles.fullText:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a fight for political survival on Tuesday in an election seen by many Israelis as the most consequential in the country's history and a referendum on his leadership since the 2023 Hamas-led attacks.

The vote follows a turbulent period for Israel, shaped by the trauma of the October 7 attacks, wars in Gaza, Lebanon and with Iran, deepening international isolation, and the divisive policies of Netanyahu's right-wing coalition.

Yet Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, remains a formidable survivor, with nationalist politics increasingly entrenched and Israel's fragmented system potentially leaving him best placed to form a government.

Opinion polls show a close race between Netanyahu's Likud Party and its right-wing allies and a rival alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and security hawk with backers on the right and in the centre.

Voters began casting ballots after polling stations opened at 7am (0500 GMT).

The polls close at 10pm (2000 GMT).

Netanyahu has campaigned on his wartime leadership and his alliance with US President Donald Trump, who has endorsed him and joined Israel in waging war on Iran.

Netanyahu said on Sunday that Trump was prepared to act again to "finally" remove the Iranian threat, but only if Netanyahu remained in power.

Eisenkot has accused Netanyahu of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies and threats" and said he was confident Trump would work "in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people".

Netanyahu may again depend on far-right leaders Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich to form a government.

Both have faced sanctions from some Western countries that accuse them of inciting violence against Palestinians, while Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power Party has gained support in opinion polls.

Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to power.

If neither can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held next year.

The Israeli Central Election Committee said 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote, some 330,000 of them for the first time.

For many of Netanyahu's opponents, the election turns on accountability for the security failures of October 7, Israel's deadliest day.

Opposition groups have promised a national inquiry.

Eldad Shaaltiel, a volunteer with Eisenkot's Yashar Party, said he had come early to hang campaign posters outside a Jerusalem polling station, aiming to sway the potentially critical pool of still wavering voters.

Some 13 percent of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Centre for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute.

Nilli Mor, a volunteer for the Democrats Party led by former general Yair Golan, another opponent of Netanyahu, said she was campaigning "to try and bring a new day to Israel, a better day with hope and great change for this country".

A high turnout among voters from Israel's Arab minority – Israeli by citizenship but Palestinian by heritage – could help nudge Israel's complex coalition arithmetic in favour of Eisenkot.

Though Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, analysts see a scenario where they could prop up a minority government he leads in order to ensure Netanyahu is removed from office.

But Ben-Gvir, casting his vote in the Kiryat Arba settlement in the occupied West Bank early on Tuesday, predicted Netanyahu would return as prime minister, adding: "We will serve as the right-wing anchor of that government".

In some bastions of Likud support, disenchanted voters have been going door to door to turn voters against Netanyahu.

Some have turned away from Netanyahu as he battles corruption charges he denies in a long-running criminal trial.

"My expectation is that we will have only a slight majority either way. No landslide," said Israeli political analyst Amotz Asa-El of the Shalom Hartman Institute. (Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
articles.excerpt: Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances…
articles.fullText:
Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade.

As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure.

Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits. Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity.

These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission. But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid.

The grid’s backbone

Moving electricity through the grid isn’t perfectly efficient: As electricity flows through power lines, some gets lost as heat. How much varies—the higher the voltage, the lower the current, and the less electricity gets lost. So a key function for the grid is stepping voltage up and down.

Consider, for example, your local solar plant. For that electricity to efficiently travel to your home hundreds of miles away, it needs to reach a higher voltage than what’s generated by the solar plant. Enter transformers.

In its path from the power plant to your outlets, electricity might go through one transformer at the solar farm and another at a substation nearby, stepping up the voltage twice to reach a high enough level to travel on high-voltage transmission lines. Solar panels also produce direct current (DC) electricity, which needs to be converted to alternating current (AC) via an inverter before it flows into a transformer. Closer to its destination, the voltage will be stepped down again, probably at least twice: once at another substation and again at a smaller transformer in your neighborhood.

If you’re in the US, electricity from a solar plant might be converted to AC by an inverter at around 480 volts, get stepped up to 115,000 volts for the transmission lines, and finally get stepped back down to 120 volts and 240 volts for your home.

Conventional transformers do this work using what essentially amount to loops of wire. The core of a transformer is typically made of a special type of steel called grain-oriented electrical steel. Coils of copper wire sit on either end of that core.

The number of loops in each coil determines the voltage on either end of the transformer: If there are more loops on the secondary coil than the primary, the voltage steps up, and if there are fewer, it steps down. When incoming electricity passes through loops on the upstream end of the transformer, that forms a magnetic field in the core. That field induces a voltage in the loops on the other side of the device, which is what allows the energy to continue flowing at a new voltage. This process is called magnetic induction.

Transformers form the backbone of electricity transmission and distribution, says Srdjan Lukic, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at North Carolina State University. In addition to doing the job of stepping up and down voltage, transformers also often provide what’s called galvanic isolation, meaning there’s no direct electrical path flowing through them. That can help limit disturbances from moving through the grid, improving safety.

The problem is that today’s transformers are big and bulky, and they’re also difficult and expensive to replace, Lukic says.

A solid option

Solid-state transformers essentially add so-called power electronics—semiconductors that convert and control electricity to the typical blueprint of today’s transformers.

While a conventional transformer operates at the frequency of the part of the grid it’s connected to, a solid-state transformer actually controls the frequency of the current. Typically, a solid-state transformer first converts incoming AC power from the grid to DC power, and then to a higher-frequency AC power using switches made of a semiconductor like silicon carbide.

From there, a magnetic component changes the voltage. Because the advanced semiconductors allow transformers to exert so much control over the frequency and stability of the current, the magnetic core can be much smaller than in a conventional transformer. Some come in at roughly one-tenth the size but have the same capacity, Lukic says.

Finally, additional power electronics convert the electricity from high-frequency AC to its required form—generally back to DC power and finally to lower-frequency AC.

Today, stepping voltage up and down is many transformers’ only job. But solid-state transformers can do much more. They absorb the jobs of devices like rectifiers and inverters (which convert AC to DC power and vice versa), shrinking the total footprint of the electrical equipment and potentially cutting the amount of power lost in the system.

In August, the New York Power Authority and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) tested a one-megawatt solid-state transformer under realistic utility conditions at EPRI’s test site. The device was built in Lukic’s lab, and it was the first such test for a transformer of that capacity, he says. 

The prototype was roughly 98% efficient—meaning it lost only 2% of the energy fed in. An equivalent conventional transformer and rectifier, by comparison, would be about 96% efficient together, Lukic says. A difference of 2% might seem small, but it is significant, since it means the solid-state transformer could cut power losses from conventional equipment in half, Lukic says.

One major goal of the project was to help utilities gain more confidence in these new components, Lukic says. That’s crucial, since these devices could be used on the power grid in the future. In the near term, solid-state transformers could be used within data centers to provide electricity for server racks.

The prototype is still a relatively low-voltage system, operating at about 15,000 volts. Industrial facilities like larger data centers often require higher-voltage connections, and transmission lines typically operate at hundreds of thousands of volts. Adapting solid-state transformers to these higher voltages will require further engineering development. But the test was a successful demonstration that solid-state transformers can work under real conditions, Lukic says.

Companies developing solid-state transformers are largely focused on data centers right now, Lukic says. There’s an influx of money to support developing the new technology, and the voltage requirements aren’t as high as they will be for larger transformers that will be needed for long-distance transmission.

In February, Heron Power raised $140 million to commercialize its solid-state transformer, which the company calls the Heron Link. The technology could be used in data centers, solar power arrays, and grid batteries, says Drew Baglino, the founder and CEO. The company is starting to test its technology at larger scales now, Baglino says. Ten megawatt-hours’ worth of batteries at Heron’s headquarters in Scotts Valley, California, will soon undergo testing with Heron transformers. The company is also planning a pilot with a nearby solar farm, Baglino says.

One challenge for solid-state transformers is that their power electronics have more failure modes than conventional transformers. In a traditional device, a failure means that the entire device will typically be taken offline, resulting in power interruptions. But Heron designs with that in mind, Baglino says: The company uses a modular design, with many small devices that work together. If one fails, the rest of the system keeps working until the affected bit can be replaced, which doesn’t require shutting the whole thing down.

Heron Power is currently building a $100 million factory in California to make advanced transformers. The facility should begin production in 2027 and reach its full production rate of 40 gigawatts’ worth of transformers per year in 2029.

The future of the grid

In recent years, companies that make grid equipment have put $1.7 billion into the US supply chain for power transformers, which are used in high-voltage transmission, says Benjamin Boucher, a supply chain analyst at Wood Mackenzie. There’s been an additional $1.3 billion invested for distribution transformers, the smaller devices that help transform power for homes and businesses, he adds.

But even this investment isn’t keeping pace with the rapid growth of the grid. Wait times for large conventional transformers—the kind needed to connect new power plants, long-distance transmission, and high-demand sites like data centers—are stretching as long as five years.

“Transformers have become one of the biggest bottlenecks for utilities, generation developers, and even data centers,” Boucher says. The big challenge is that it’s difficult to get new transformer manufacturing up and running, because it’s a quite technical process that requires a lot of specialized labor. So even facilities announced years ago are still years from opening, Boucher says.

Solid-state transformers could help ease some of that pressure. But high-voltage devices needed for power plant connections and transmission lines are the holy grail for solid-state transformers, Lukic says. Existing solid-state technology can’t be used for those applications yet, so the industry will need to develop new materials and designs to support high voltages and handle electricity safely in a compact device.

“We’re facing a big risk related to grid infrastructure,” Boucher says. “Without the transformers, you don’t really have an electrical grid.”

articles.title: Foreign Ministry chides Mbappe over Mao comments
articles.excerpt: The Foreign Ministry in Beijing on Tuesday said that hurting the feelings of the country's people would meet "unanimous rejection"…
articles.fullText:
The Foreign Ministry in Beijing on Tuesday said that hurting the feelings of the country's people would meet "unanimous rejection" after football star Kylian Mbappe's comments about former leader Mao Zedong.

The French footballer's recent comments, in which he appeared to mock the founding leader of the People's Republic of China, resulted in two major Chinese brands dropping their sponsorship deals with the player.

"We have seen the relevant reports. Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with unanimous rejection from all sectors of Chinese society," Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing.

"Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments," drinks giant Dongpeng said in a statement, adding that "with immediate effect we are terminating all cooperation with Kylian Mbappe".

Mengniu, China's largest dairy producer, also cut ties with the Real Madrid forward.

Mbappe apologised for his comment in a statement put out later on Tuesday.

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone my words have upset.

"This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry. (Additional reporting by AFP)

articles.title: Water pipe burst in Shau Kei Wan affects 10k homes
articles.excerpt: The Water Supplies Department on Tuesday said more than 10,000 homes in Shau Kei Wan and its nearby areas saw…
articles.fullText:
The Water Supplies Department on Tuesday said more than 10,000 homes in Shau Kei Wan and its nearby areas saw their fresh water supply suspended following a water pipe burst.

The burst occurred at around 10.30am at a construction site along Shau Kei Wan Road.

Speaking to reporters, Chief Engineer of Hong Kong and Islands Region Lin Tang-tai said the department aimed to resume water supply by midnight.

He said the pipe concerned, with a diametre of 18 inches, had been in use for more than three decades.

But the incident was not caused by ageing, instead it was due to external forces, he said, with the crack measuring over one metre.

“The scope of the impact involved in the incident covered Shau Kei Wan and parts of Sai Wan Ho. The number of households involved exceeds 10,000," he said.

"We will deploy more than 10 water trucks, 100 water tanks and tens of thousands of bottled water, as well as various supporting facilities, to provide temporary fresh water supplies for residents affected.”

The Highways Department, for its part, apologised for the inconvenience caused.

Chief Highway Engineer Alan Chan said contractors had already carried out an inspection ahead of the construction work, adding that his department would look into the cause of the incident and see if the contractors are liable.

Police said a care home resident in her 80s was hospitalised after she sustained injuries to her limbs due to the incident.

A member of staff told RTHK that the victim yelled for help when one of the care home’s windows cracked due to the burst pipe, shooting sand and water into one of the rooms.

Meanwhile, Eastern District care teams were seen assisting the public at one of the water collection points where at least dozens of people were in the queue.

A resident surnamed Law told RTHK she planned to come down twice to take sufficient water for cooking first.

“Of course I am upset there is no water supply. Water is very crucial, right? Being unable to bathe after work is very uncomfortable," she said.

Another resident said he was not too optimistic that fresh water supply could resume by midnight, adding his family might go out for dinner instead of cooking at home.

In a statement, lawmaker Elaine Chik said the incident showed that the authorities’ information on underground pipes was not accurate enough, and that pre-construction detection also required improvements.

She urged authorities to review its underground facilities management, saying they should establish a database for such utilities.

articles.title: Three nabbed in wounding case linked to illegal fuel
articles.excerpt: Police said they have arrested three men for allegedly conspiring to wound with intent in a case that might involve…
articles.fullText:
Police said they have arrested three men for allegedly conspiring to wound with intent in a case that might involve illicit fuel activity.

Officers were alerted by staff at Tseung Kwan O Hospital in the early hours last Thursday that a 35-year-old light goods vehicle driver – who sought treatment at the hospital – suffered knife wounds.

Speaking in a media briefing on Tuesday, inspector Fong Miu-kwan said preliminary investigations revealed that he was attacked on Chun Yat Street at Tseung Kwan O Industrial Estate.

Fong said authorities found 120 litres of suspected illicit fuel in his vehicle.

The three suspects are aged 16 to 19 with suspected triad background.

“According to the police investigation, the place where the incident occurred – Tseung Kwan O Industrial Estate – has seen illicit fuel activities in the past," Fong said.

"Police have not ruled out the possibility that the wounding case was linked to a dispute over illicit fuel transactions.”

In a separate case, authorities found 750 litres of suspected illicit diesel in a medium goods vehicle as part of their campaign against illegal fuel activity at Tseung Kwan O Industrial Estate, and a 25-year-old driver is suspected of involvement.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: HSBC net profit rises in Q3 but misses forecasts
articles.excerpt: Banking giant HSBC on Tuesday said net profit in the third quarter rose a less-than-expected 45.5 percent year-on-year as the…
articles.fullText:
Banking giant HSBC on Tuesday said net profit in the third quarter rose a less-than-expected 45.5 percent year-on-year as the London-headquartered lender continued to restructure operations and cut costs.

Profit attributable to shareholders for the three months ending in September stood at US$7 billion, from US$4.87 billion a year earlier, HSBC said in a filing to the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Pre-tax profit grew 32 percent to US$9.6 billion, with revenue increasing by US$0.8 billion to US$18.6 billion.

"As we simplify HSBC, we are creating greater capacity to invest, grow and deliver strong returns for our shareholders," chief executive Georges Elhedery said in the filing.

The banking giant also approved a third interim dividend of US$0.10 per share, and announced second US$1 billion buyback after completing one in the previous three months.

HSBC said it remained "confident in achieving the targets" set out earlier this year.

"We continue to target year-on-year growth in revenue from 2026 to 2028, rising to five percent growth in 2028 compared with 2027," it said.

The bank also said expected credit losses tumbled 17 percent to US$800 million from the same period a year ago, thanks to a reduction in charges linked to Hong Kong's real estate sector as well as its UK and Mexican wealth businesses.

The lender also said it expected net interest income of at least US$46 billion for 2025. (Agencies)

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Brewers rout Rays to reach brink of World Series sweep
articles.excerpt: With a devastating 16-hit batting performance and masterful pitching by Robert Gasser, the Milwaukee Brewers routed Tampa Bay 10-1 on…
articles.fullText:
With a devastating 16-hit batting performance and masterful pitching by Robert Gasser, the Milwaukee Brewers routed Tampa Bay 10-1 on Monday, reaching the brink of a World Series sweep.

Left-handed starter Gasser threw six shutout innings, allowing only one hit with a walk and three strikeouts in facing the minimum 18 batters.

"It was awesome," Gasser said.

"We're going to enjoy tonight. It was a great team win. But we've got work to do."

Jackson Chourio, a 22-year-old Venezuelan outfielder, went 4-for-5 at the plate, scored twice, stole a base and also drove in a run in the Brewers' historic eight-run fifth inning to humble the Rays.

All eight runs came with two outs in the inning, a World Series record, and Milwaukee batters made seven consecutive hits, a playoff first.

"It was special for sure," Chourio said through a translator.

"We've been preparing for this day. We've known it was coming. We have one more to lock in for tomorrow to complete the mission."

The Brewers seized a 3-0 lead in Major League Baseball's best-of-seven final and can win the first title in team history with a triumph in game four on Tuesday at Tropicana Field.

"There's still one more game to go for us to win," Gasser said.

"I know everybody is eager to do it and we're going to show up tomorrow ready to go."

Gasser became the first lefty to face the minimum over six innings in a World Series clash since Sandy Koufax of the Los Angeles Dodgers in 1965.

The Rays managed a run in the ninth but only three hits in the game.

Chourio raced home from second base on a Christian Yelich single in the third inning to score the first run and William Contreras drove in another with a hit to right field for a 2-0 lead.

The Brewers, whose only prior World Series was a 1982 loss to St. Louis in seven games, had two one-run wins to start the Series but overwhelmed Tampa Bay with a barrage in the fifth.

Chourio singled, stole second and advanced to third on a Contreras single that loaded the bases as Rays starter Freddy Peralta, who had played for Milwaukee the past eight seasons, was lifted for relief pitcher Cam Booser.

Brice Turang followed with a two-run single up the middle, Garrett Mitchell added a single to score Contreras, and Cooper Pratt followed with a two-run double to left field for a 7-0 Brewers lead.

Sal Frelick doubled in Pratt for an 8-0 Milwaukee edge, bringing on Rays reliever Cole Sulser, who promptly surrendered a single to David Hamilton to drive in Frelick for a 9-0 lead.

Chourio concluded the stunning streak with a double to right field to score Hamilton for a 10-0 Brewers lead.

Gasser, meanwhile, had to wait an extra 45 minutes before returning to the mound, watching the amazing streak with glee.

"It was special. I had a smile on my face the whole time," Gasser said.

"It was just surreal when something like that happens."

Chourio's eight hits through three games are the second-most in World Series history after nine by Billy Hatcher for Cincinnati in 1990.

"My mentality is to stay on top of the ball and hit line drives," Chourio said.

"I consider myself more of a hitter than a home run hitter."

Chourio became the youngest player to ever begin a World Series with three multi-hit games, delivering singles in the first, third and fifth innings on Monday. (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Over 1,600 affected in airline, retailer data breaches
articles.excerpt: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data on Tuesday confirmed that more than 1,600 people have been affected…
articles.fullText:
The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data on Tuesday confirmed that more than 1,600 people have been affected by data breaches at Hong Kong Airlines and electronics retailer Yoho Hong Kong.

The privacy watchdog said the breach at Hong Kong Airlines affected 815 passengers travelling between September 29 and October 22, involving their names, phone numbers and flight information.

The Yoho Hong Kong breach affected 790 customers who placed their orders between September 29 and October 12, involving their names, phone numbers along with delivery information.

The watchdog said customers received suspected scam calls stating their personal data.

Additionally, the privacy commissioner received a data-breach incident report from Broadway Photo Supply.

As of Monday, it had received a total of 23 complaints and 20 inquiries, and investigations have been launched.

The office urged people to consider carefully should they have any doubts about callers claiming to be merchants, and verify their identities and authenticity of the calls through official channels.

Customers should also refuse any suspicious money-transfer requests and keep records of communications.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: CUHK to bid for Hung Shui Kiu university town land
articles.excerpt: Chinese University of Hong Kong will bid for one of the first three sites in the Northern Metropolis University Town…
articles.fullText:
Chinese University of Hong Kong will bid for one of the first three sites in the Northern Metropolis University Town in Hung Shui Kiu, Vice-Chancellor Professor Dennis Lo said, but warned that the government's staggered tendering process and high construction costs pose major challenges.

In an interview with Ming Pao published on Tuesday, Lo said the university town project would allow the city's eight publicly funded universities to expand their footprint and increase their impact on society.

"Our campus is currently relatively small, like a boutique hotel, and I believe this Northern Metropolis University Town has given us a rare opportunity to have some land to expand our footprint," he said.

He said Hong Kong universities enjoy strong international reputations and high rankings but are limited in size.

Lo said scale is important for universities to produce research that can "change the world", as campus size affects the number of researchers, which in turn affects patents and publications.

The university town would help break through the space constraint, he said.

He noted that the university had established an InnoHub for New Quality Industries in Qianhai, near Hung Shui Kiu, in March this year, and believed there would be synergy effects.

He said the university was considering collaboration with overseas institutions and industries in future at the Hung Shui Kiu university town, but could not reveal further details as it was competing with other universities.

However, Lo predicted that due to limited land, the university may prefer to set up research institutes rather than full campuses in the university town.

He also said the government's plan to tender the three campuses — in Hung Shui Kiu, San Tin and Ta Kwu Ling — at different times would make planning and collaboration among universities more difficult.

"The three plots are being rolled out in batches. For the first ones, you dare not not bid, because each time is an opportunity," he said.

On financing, Lo said CUHK would be prudent with possible future development at the Northern Metropolis.

He noted that while the government has earmarked HK$10 billion for loans to support campus development at the Northern Metropolis University Town, there is a cap on borrowing and construction costs are high.

He estimated that HK$10 billion would only be enough to build five buildings, and called on the government to increase funding.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Chinese industrial profits see sharp rise to 14.4pc
articles.excerpt: China's industrial profits grew at a faster pace in September, though a deepening divergence across the economy continued to weigh…
articles.fullText:
China's industrial profits grew at a faster pace in September, though a deepening divergence across the economy continued to weigh on business earnings.

Profits at industrial firms rose 14.4 percent from a year earlier last month, quickening from a 4.2 increase in August, data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed on Tuesday.

Profits were up 15.5 percent in the first nine months, compared with a 15.7 percent increase in the January-August period.

While export-oriented firms brace for greater uncertainty, as expanding trade surpluses heighten the risk of external pressures, firms tied to domestic demand continue to grapple with subdued consumption, casting a shadow over the sustainability of profit growth.

The sectoral divide remained pronounced.

Profits in the computer, communication, and other electronic equipment manufacturing category soared 103.8 percent in the first nine months, whereas the furniture manufacturing sector posted a 51.3 percent decline, making it one of the weakest performers and highlighting the uneven nature of China's economy.

A stronger-than-expected 4.5 percent expansion in the third quarter put China within reach of its annual growth target of 4.5 to five percent, but disparities across different parts of the economy suggest the recovery remains unbalanced, with persistent weakness in some sectors continuing to erode corporate profitability.

That pressure has become increasingly visible at the company level.

Net profit at the world's largest electric vehicle battery maker, CATL, slowed sharply in the past quarter, as intense competition in the EV battery market squeezed margins at a time when China's auto sales were in a downturn.

Industrial profit figures cover firms with yearly revenue of at least 20 million yuan from main operations. (Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: CE homes in on N Metropolis vigour in call to top unis
articles.excerpt: Chief Executive John Lee has called on global university leaders to join the SAR’s Northern Metropolis development, saying it is…
articles.fullText:
Chief Executive John Lee has called on global university leaders to join the SAR’s Northern Metropolis development, saying it is where the future of education, research, industry and technology lies.

In an opening speech at the Global University Presidents and Leaders Summit at the Convention and Exhibition Centre on Tuesday, he said Hong Kong, with a total land area of about 1,100 square kilometres, is home to five institutions that are ranked among the world’s top 100.

The Northern Metropolis mega project lies at the core of Hong Kong’s future, with its main focus being the university towns that will be springing up, he said.

Lee said the mega project's university towns of San Tin, Hung Shui Kiu and Ta Kwu Ling are positioned to attract the world’s best scholars and students and that they would each have a distinct focus.

“The towns are also designed to empower industry,” he said.

“We will encourage university staff to undertake research at companies. We will encourage industry professionals to contribute to university teaching and research.

“Our goal is to strengthen the links between industry, academia and research – enabling them to complement and reinforce one another.”

The government will also invite universities to establish basic research institutes and large-scale shared research platforms at the university towns, Lee added.

The two-day event in Wan Chai has attracted more than 50 renowned university leaders from more than 20 countries and regions.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: HK rises amid Anthropic IPO lift for regional markets
articles.excerpt: Asian stocks surged on Tuesday as AI bellwether Anthropic's eagerly anticipated IPO filing lifted risk appetite ahead of tech earnings…
articles.fullText:
Asian stocks surged on Tuesday as AI bellwether Anthropic's eagerly anticipated IPO filing lifted risk appetite ahead of tech earnings that will be a test for the AI trade, and central bank meetings that will influence near-term interest rates.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index opened up 48 points, or 0.21 percent, at 23,260.

The China enterprises index was 14 points, or 0.18 percent, higher at 7,816 while the tech index rose 28 points, or 0.74 percent, to 3,886.

Across the border, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index opened up 0.02 percent at 3,698.

The Shenzhen Component Index opened almost 57 points, or 0.49 percent, higher at 11,591 while the ChiNext Index was up 0.89 percent, to open at 2,661.

The gains in Hong Kong and the mainland came as US Claude-owner Anthropic disclosed a steep loss and red-hot revenue growth in its filing for a US initial public offering, as investors increasingly dissect the potential payoff from massive AI spending and its profitability.

Also boosting sentiment was Meta Platforms' plans to raise up to US$95 billion in its largest-ever equity fundraising.

The currency markets are muted ahead of policy decisions from the US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan, with economists expecting all three to stand pat on interest rates, leaving the focus on comments from policymakers to gauge the rates outlook.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei opened 379 points, or 0.61 percent, up at 62,569 before the gains piled on to send the 225 benchmark 1,168 points higher at one stage before noon as Anthropic's IPO filing and gains in the US semiconductor index lifted local AI-related stocks.

In Seoul, the Kospi surged 189 points, or 3.46 percent, up to open at 5,658 and was 226 points higher at one stage before lunch, taking the lead from US artificial intelligence gains and strong local economic growth data.

More than a third of US S&P 500 companies are scheduled to report earnings this week, including hyperscalers Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon.com.

"Given the increased AI scrutiny of late and circular arrangements, investors will want evidence that demand is broadening beyond these interconnected relationships to support the continued infrastructure expansion," said Anthony Saglimbene, Ameriprise's chief market strategist.

"Investors need confidence that aggressive capex spending reflects durable business needs and that profitability will hold up as new infrastructure comes into service," he said.

Fed policymakers have telegraphed they will not raise short-term borrowing costs again this week, but with inflation concerns still front and centre, investors believe a rate-hike pause will not last for long. Traders are pricing in a hike from the Fed in December.

"Can we expect [US] growth to hold up in an environment of higher rates? We think yes. We believe the US economy is going to be able to manage through higher interest rates," said Geng Ngarmboonanant, head of macro and policy, multi-asset solutions, JP Morgan Asset Management. (Reuters/Xinhua)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Truce begins in Russian-occupied city in Kherson
articles.excerpt: A truce between Ukraine and Russia aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky came into force…
articles.fullText:
A truce between Ukraine and Russia aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky came into force on Tuesday, having been announced by US First Lady Melania Trump last week.

Both sides said earlier they would observe the truce starting at 3am local time, or 9am Hong Kong time.

Soon after the appointed time, Russia's defence ministry said it had suspended strikes on the region.

The war-ravaged city in Ukraine's southern Kherson region has been caught in the crosshairs of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces at the start of the conflict.

Former residents said earlier this year that those remaining in the city were starving, lacked medicine and could not easily leave.

The ceasefire, which applies to a limited area, comes as the Ukraine war grinds through its fifth year.

Three-way peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv are set to resume in November after a months-long hiatus.

Neither Russia, Ukraine nor the United States has said who would monitor the truce, or given details about the humanitarian operation set to accompany it.

Announcing last Friday that she had brokered the ceasefire, Melania Trump said civilian officials from both Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes and "determine the level of assistance they require".

Neither Russia nor Ukraine has said how long the truce would last.

The Russian defence ministry said on Friday it would halt fire in the "Kherson sector" for the duration of the ceasefire, without giving details.

The city, on the southern bank of the Dnipro River, has seen its population drop from about 24,000 before the conflict to around 2,000.

Those remaining include up to 50 children, according to Ukrainian and US estimates.

Former residents told AFP earlier this year that people still living in the city were forced to hunt pigeons or survive on whatever they had in their garden.

The city was heavily damaged by the 2023 destruction of the Kakhovka dam, which unleashed major flooding along the Dnipro River. (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Walter Koenig of 'Star Trek' fame dies at 90
articles.excerpt: Walter Koenig, the actor best known for his role as Pavel Chekov on the groundbreaking television show "Star Trek" and…
articles.fullText:
Walter Koenig, the actor best known for his role as Pavel Chekov on the groundbreaking television show "Star Trek" and in the franchise's first seven movies, has died at age 90, his representative said on Monday.

Koenig died at his home in North Hollywood in Los Angeles, his agent Zachery McGinnis said in a statement, citing the cause of "old age" without further details.

The actor was known for playing the youthful Russian navigator Chekov in the original television series, as well as in several "Star Trek" feature films.

"Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world," read the statement.

"Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before."

The actor died surrounded by his daughter and niece, added the statement.

Ensign Pavel Chekov first appeared in the iconic series at the start of its second season, in 1967.

The character was meant to appeal to younger viewers.

William Shatner, who played Captain James T Kirk, and Leonard Nimoy (Mr. Spock) were both in their mid-thirties at the onset of the series, nearly over the hill by the era's standards.

Koenig was 30 when he was cast, and producers hoped he'd appeal to teens, with his mop-top hairstyle not unlike Davy Jones of the Monkees, the famed TV-produced pop band.

Born in Chicago and raised in Manhattan, Koenig was the child of Lithuanian immigrants.

He earned a bachelor's degree in psychology and initially planned a career as a psychiatrist.

But acting proved a good bet.

"Star Trek" was given a tepid reception when it debuted, but it eventually snowballed into a cultural phenomenon, spawning a universe of spinoff series along with the films, and a rabid fan following.

The original show ran from 1966 to 1969.

Koenig told The Los Angeles Times that when it was cancelled he was "totally at sea" with "no reason to get up in the morning".

But the series soon found massive cult fame, with "Trekkie" super fans who have kept it alive to this day.

Koenig signed on to a film franchise that followed, becoming a mainstay of "Star Trek" movies released between 1979 and 1994.

He also appeared in non-canon spin-offs, and was in the space drama TV series "Babylon 5".

Throughout his career he also posted a number of writing credits, and also worked on computer games.

Koenig married Judy Levitt, who also appeared in "Star Trek" films, in 1965.

She died in 2022.

"My heart is heavy," wrote George Takei, Koenig's "Star Trek" co-star who played Sulu in the franchise.

"Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too," Takei wrote on Facebook.

"Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course." (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Syria shuts border crossing with Jordan after strikes
articles.excerpt: Jordan said on Monday its air force struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that…
articles.fullText:
Jordan said on Monday its air force struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week's deadly church attack in the kingdom were linked to "terrorist groups" operating there.

The armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus. Syria's government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas.

Damascus informed Jordan of its "complete reservation" over the strikes without prior coordination, the foreign ministry said in a statement.

Seven people, including three children and a woman, were killed and three others were wounded in the Jordanian strikes, the Syrian Civil Defence said in a preliminary report. It said emergency teams responded to four sites hit by the strikes in the countryside of Daraa and Sweida provinces.

There was no immediate comment from Jordan on that account.

Shortly after the strikes, Syria closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Tuesday, suspending passenger and commercial traffic in both directions, citing developments on the ground in Daraa province, the Syrian General Authority for Border Crossings and Customs said in a statement.

Nassib is Jordan's only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria.

Earlier on Monday, senior government security officials said Jordanian security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law after a shootout on Monday over the church violence that killed nine people.

"God willing, they only represent themselves," said Jordan's Director of Public Security, Major-General Obeidallah al-Maaytah.

Such violence is rare in Jordan, a relatively stable US ally in the Middle East. Friday's attack on the Christian minority prompted King Abdullah to order security forces to respond with an "iron fist".

In a press conference, al-Maaytah and Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said the country would not tolerate extremist terrorism.

"The file has not yet been closed; investigations are still ongoing. As of today, there are no indications of any links between them and other cells," al-Faraya added.

Friday's assault during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud, about 120 km southwest of the capital, Amman, also wounded at least 34 people. Witnesses said gunmen opened fire for several minutes.

The suspects, who lived near Hamoud, will face justice, said the security officials. The three suspects were named in the press briefing.

Jordan's Public Security Directorate said in a statement carried by state media that security forces located the suspects while they were hiding in an abandoned house. They refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after wounding them.

No security personnel were injured, and security forces found a number of firearms and rounds of ammunition in the suspects' possession.

There has been no claim of responsibility for the church attack.

Jordan, a US partner in the fight against extremism, has foiled Islamist militant plots in the past. The security officials did not name any Islamist groups in the press conference. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Brazil election looks rigged, says Trump
articles.excerpt: US President Donald Trump said on Monday that leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's surprise win in Brazil's presidential…
articles.fullText:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's surprise win in Brazil's presidential vote "looked like another rigged election," although the party of defeated right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result.

The son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat in Sunday's presidential election, saying he would seek the annulment of Lula's victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours.

Later on Monday, however, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party said it acknowledged the runoff result in a statement signed by the party's head Valdemar Costa Neto.

"We recognise the presidential election results," Costa Neto said. "But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified."

Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party's statement, said earlier on Monday he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil.

Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.

"I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. "It looked very bad to me."

Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that it will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03 percent of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.

"I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated," Trump said. "The extension given was very strange."

Vice President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil's electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump's remarks were "totally wrong" and "unfounded."

Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil's former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula.

Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022.

World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with dismay by investors who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win.

Brazil's real fell 8.1 percent against the US dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020.

"The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure," said Pantheon Macroeconomics' chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia.

Lula's victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.

Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved social media campaign helped power Lula to victory. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Ex-FBI chief Comey faces third prosecution attempt
articles.excerpt: The US Justice Department is attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey for a third time, the latest case…
articles.fullText:
The US Justice Department is attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey for a third time, the latest case accusing him of sharing sensitive national security information in 2016, according to court documents made public on Monday.

The case was revealed in a court document known as a "criminal information" that the Justice Department said it filed to stop the 10-year statute of limitations on the offence from expiring earlier this month.

The document filed in Washington federal court charges Comey with transmitting and conspiring to transmit national defence information. It alleges he shared classified information with a reporter from the New York Times in October 2016.

Comey said in a video on Instagram that "they're back again" and referenced the Justice Department, but did not provide further details. "I'm still innocent," he added. Comey's lawyers have already asked a judge to dismiss the case, arguing it is legally improper.

The new case adds to the legal fights facing Comey, whom the Justice Department has already charged twice, accusing him of lying to Congress about media leaks and threatening US President Donald Trump in a social media post. A judge dismissed the false statements case, while the threats case remains pending.

Comey's lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that the document "purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit." The criminal information was filed on October 5, but was unsealed on Monday at the request of Comey's lawyers.

A Justice Department spokesperson described the manoeuvre to halt the statute of limitations as a "widely recognised practice in federal court."

"This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," the spokesperson said in a statement. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Kane, Putellas win top honours at 2026 Ballon d'Or
articles.excerpt: Harry Kane became England's first Ballon d'Or winner in 25 years in his native city of London on Monday, beating…
articles.fullText:
Harry Kane became England's first Ballon d'Or winner in 25 years in his native city of London on Monday, beating out stiff competition from Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.

Alexia Putellas claimed the women's prize for a third time to extend Spain's domination of the award, thanks to her role in leading Barcelona to last season's Champions League before moving to London City Lionesses.

The first ever Ballon d'Or ceremony on English soil got off to an inauspicious start as the London traffic caused a delay of nearly an hour, with many of the star names arriving late.

But there was a happy ending for the hometown hero as Kane collected the crowning glory of his career to date.

The 33-year-old Bayern Munich forward struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, propelling the German giants to a league and cup double.

He also scored six times as England finished third at the World Cup.

"Without you guys (his Bayern Munich teammates) and the rest of the team it wouldn't be possible, the way you guys push me, the way we compete. So thank you very much," he said after collecting the award.

Kane's medal collection is limited to German domestic triumphs since he arrived at Bayern in 2023.

He was on the losing side for Tottenham in the 2019 Champions League final against Liverpool and twice tasted bitter defeat in the final of the European Championship with England.

But his remarkable goalscoring consistency has earned him the highest individual award in football.

"Making the move to Bayern Munich was a big step in my career," Kane told AFP earlier. "Some people saw it as a risk but for me it was always about improving and seeing if I could get better around the teammates, the team, the club and it has pushed me onto another level.

"Being a number nine for Bayern and England you are expected to score goals and to do that the number of times I did last year is something I'm really proud of," he added.

Winner in 2021 and 2022, Putellas's third Ballon d'Or caps her return back to the top of the women's game after an anterior cruciate ligament injury derailed her rise four years ago.

Putellas succeeds Spain teammate Aitana Bonmati, the winner the past three years who was sidelined by a leg break for most of last season.

"Ever since I suffered the injury, I've been trying to enjoy every moment as if it were my last, because you never know if it'll happen again," Putellas told AFP in an interview last month.

"I never felt that the (Ballon d'Or) trophy was 'mine'... Having already experienced it once, I'm able to enjoy it even more now," she added.

Yamal made the boldest fashion statement of the contenders with a pink flower on the front of his black suit.

The Barcelona winger scooped up the first award of the night for young talent of the year for the third consecutive time.

But the 19-year-old fell short of becoming the youngest ever Ballon d'Or winner after he failed to produce his best form during Spain's World Cup success.

Mbappe got the better of Yamal with two goals as Real Madrid edged Barcelona 2-1 in El Clasico on Sunday.

But his wait to win the Ballon d'Or goes on despite his prolific year for France and Real Madrid.

Luis de la Fuente beat out Paris Saint-Germain's Luis Enrique and Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta to be named men's coach of the year after leading Spain to World Cup glory.

"I'm really privileged to work with a team of such high quality on a professional and human level," said de la Fuente.

Barcelona's Pere Romeu scooped the prize for women's coach of the year.

Arsenal's Bukayo Saka won the Socrates award for his humanitarian work.
