Paris Saint-Germain missed out on any of the main individual awards despite winning a second consecutive Champions League, but did have the consolation of men's club of the year.

Spanish duo Unai Simon and Cata Coll were named best men's and women's goalkeeper. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Trump pledges million-dollar voter fraud reward
articles.excerpt: US President Donald Trump on Monday announced a US$1 million reward for information about voter fraud, in a fresh bid…
articles.fullText:
US President Donald Trump on Monday announced a US$1 million reward for information about voter fraud, in a fresh bid to sow doubt ahead of the US midterms and push his false claim about winning the 2020 election.

"Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud!" Trump wrote on his Truth Social network.

The president gave no details of how the reward would be funded or administered.

With the November 3 elections just eight days away, polls show Democrats pulling ahead as Republicans fight to retain control of both chambers of Congress.

A Democratic victory would threaten to stall Trump's agenda and expose his administration to congressional investigations during his final two years in office.

Trump has repeatedly made baseless allegations about election fraud, including his claim that he won the 2020 presidential election.

Studies have consistently found voter fraud exceptionally rare, particularly voting by non-citizens, which is already illegal in federal elections.

Trump's announcement follows a series of extraordinary pre-election promises, including an offer of US$5,000 to every adult American citizen if Republicans retain both chambers – a proposal costing more than US$1 trillion that would require congressional approval.

He has also tied compensation for veterans sickened by contaminated water at a North Carolina military base to a Republican victory.

Meanwhile, the Justice Department has sued to prevent the state of Alaska from certifying its Senate election results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses, citing possible voter confusion over another candidate with the same name.

Trump acknowledged personally ordering the lawsuit, although his attorney general denied seeking to overturn the election result.

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Microsoft offers voluntary exit deals to 60,000 staff
articles.excerpt: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, the company said on Monday, roughly a quarter of its workforce…
articles.fullText:
Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, the company said on Monday, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant seeks to cut costs while pouring money into artificial intelligence.

Staff on select teams in the United States, Canada, India and Britain at vice president level and below will be eligible, a Microsoft spokesperson said, while some groups of employees, including some working on data centres, sales and marketing, are excluded.

"The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, an executive vice president and chief people officer, told employees in a memo.

It's the second voluntary buyout offer that Microsoft has offered employees this year.

In April, the company reportedly offered around seven percent of its US workforce the option to retire early.

Around 30 percent of those eligible took the voluntary retirement plan, according to CNBC.

Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings.

Around 27 percent of Microsoft's workforce is eligible for the new buyout offer.

The company is expected to report quarterly earnings later this week. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: UN probe accuses Israel of extermination in West Bank
articles.excerpt: Israel has committed the crime against humanity of "extermination" in the West Bank, while continuing to commit "genocide" against Palestinians…
articles.fullText:
Israel has committed the crime against humanity of "extermination" in the West Bank, while continuing to commit "genocide" against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, United Nations-mandated investigators said on Monday.

The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry said Israeli forces had also committed other crimes against humanity and war crimes in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967.

The commission, which does not speak for the UN itself, first determined in a September 2025 report that Israel had committed "genocide" in the war in Gaza following Hamas's deadly October 7, 2023 attack on Israel – a finding Israel flatly rejects.

In a new report, released the day before Israel's general election, the investigation found that in the West Bank, through military operations reinforced by sustained settler violence, Israel has waged a "widespread and systematic attack" against civilians.

"The Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core," it said.

Israel rejected the allegations, with its foreign ministry on X calling it "a propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel's right to self-defence" and "legitimising jihadist terrorism".

The three-member investigative team was established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021.

South African former High Court judge Navi Pillay, who chaired the investigation until November 2025, won the Nobel Peace Prize earlier this month.

The commission's new report focused on killings and bodily and mental harm caused by both Israeli and Palestinian security forces since October 2023.

It found that the situation in the West Bank had deteriorated gravely since Hamas' attack from Gaza that month.

The commission found Israeli authorities "intended to collectively punish" West Bank civilians for the Hamas attack.

"The targeting of Palestinian civilians across different locations in the West Bank indicates a high level of coordination and organised planning and is the product of state policy," the report said.

The conduct of Israeli authorities indicates that "they knew and intended settler violence" to be part of the widespread and systematic attack, it added.

"The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel's persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unliveable," said commission chairman Srinivasan Muralidhar.

"Attempting to equate Palestinian statehood with a threat to the existence of Israel is blocking any viable attempts to realise Palestinians' right to self-determination," the Indian judge said in a statement.

The report cited cases where the commission concluded that Israeli forces intended to seriously harm and kill civilians, in acts amounting to war crimes, including wilful killing.

The October 2023 Hamas attack resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally based on official Israeli figures.

Israel's military offensive, in response, has displaced nearly the entire population of Gaza and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

"The cases investigated for this report show that the Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza," the report said.

The inquiry urged Israel to "end the commission of genocide in Gaza" and act immediately on "obligations to prevent and punish genocide and incitement to genocide".

Israel should "immediately end the unlawful occupation of Palestinian territory", and remove all settlers and settlements.

Turning to the Palestinian Authority, the report said that "Palestinian state violence has targeted and continues to target members of opposing Palestinian armed groups and repress Palestinian civil and political opposition".

The Palestinian Authority struggles with credibility and legitimacy, and "targets Palestinians who voice dissenting civil and political views... resulting in killings", it said.

"The Palestinian Authority has also failed to conduct prompt, effective and impartial investigations into incidents of killings."

There was no immediate reaction from the Palestinian Authority.

As the report was presented to the UN General Assembly in New York, Palestinian ambassador Riyad Mansour said "governments must move beyond statements and take concrete measures to protect the Palestinian people". (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Iran holds 'very good' talks with Mecca pact nations
articles.excerpt: Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan held talks with Iran on Monday in an attempt to stop the…
articles.fullText:
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan held talks with Iran on Monday in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting, with Tehran saying the discussions were "very good".

Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis", a Saudi foreign ministry statement said.

The talks, which included heavyweight Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war.

It was the first joint visit to Tehran by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye since they formed a defence alliance in Mecca, the holy city in western Saudi Arabia, in August.

The delegations met Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. The meeting ended without concrete announcements, with the various parties saying they "agreed to continue discussions" according to Iranian state media.

But Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said the discussions in the capital Tehran were "very good", according to state television.

"I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen," said the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.

He said they agreed that security in the region "should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention", saying emphasis was put on the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon, southern Syria, Gaza and the West Bank.

Prince Khalid, Pakistan's powerful army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Rezaei.

Regional tensions have risen ahead of Israel's pivotal elections on Tuesday and next week's US midterms, where US President Donald Trump's Republicans are battling to keep control of both chambers of the US Congress.

As the talks in Tehran began, United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres said it was "essential to stop any escalation" in the Middle East.

"The risk to have the combination of an overwhelming military attack on Iran, and an overwhelming military attack by Iran on the countries of the Gulf, needs to be avoided at all costs," he told a press conference in Cairo.

Fresh explosions rattled Riyadh overnight, which has suffered weeks of attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis, after the group claimed a new attack on the Saudi capital's international airport on Sunday.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen later reported intercepting three Houthi-launched drones over southern Saudi Arabia and the Riyadh region.

Responding to the weeks of attacks, Egypt's parliament approved President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to approve defensive military support for Saudi Arabia "if requested". It was not clear exactly what support was on offer.

US-Iran mediation efforts have been led by Qatar and Pakistan. A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Sunday, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: AI stocks on Wall Street lifted by Anthropic filing
articles.excerpt: US stocks closed higher on Monday, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq coming off consecutive weekly declines, as Anthropic's IPO…
articles.fullText:
US stocks closed higher on Monday, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq coming off consecutive weekly declines, as Anthropic's IPO filing helped boost sentiment in AI-related stocks in a week filled with a host of market catalysts.

Anthropic disclosed steep losses and red-hot revenue growth in its filing for a US initial public offering, laying out its ambition to build AI systems capable of reshaping the global economy despite the high costs of developing the technology.

The AI lab is pushing ahead with its listing plans even as a once-lively autumn IPO calendar has slowed, with recent market volatility prompting companies to delay offerings.

Anthropic's filing comes as investors increasingly dissect the potential pay-off from massive AI spending and at the start of an eventful week.

On tap are the Federal Reserve's policy statement on Wednesday, readings on US economic growth and inflation on Thursday and a slew of corporate earnings reports throughout the week.

More than a third of S&P 500 companies are scheduled to report earnings this week, including hyper-scalers Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, whose results will be parsed for signs of whether the hefty AI investments are translating into growth.

"Today's all about the Anthropic release, so we're back on a little bit of an optimistic tilt, I would say. But there's a lot in that release. It will be interesting to see how well things are received when they actually come to list," said JP Powers, chief investment officer at RWA Wealth Partners in Boston.

"The risk is maybe a little bit of a whipsaw if things aren't all moving in the same direction. A little optimism today, but who knows what will happen from some of these other releases this week," he said.

The S&P 500 rose 0.7 percent, to 7,676, the Nasdaq rose 0.8 percent, to 26,169, while the Dow rose 0.3 percent, to 52,361.

Semiconductor and chip-related companies, widely viewed as some of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, helped fuel the gains.

Meta shares closed down 1.9 percent after the social media company said it plans to raise up to US$95 billion in equity to fund its AI-related expansion of data centres, cloud computing power and other infrastructure.

The AI trade has come under pressure this month amid concerns that debt-funded spending may become harder to justify in the face of climbing borrowing costs.

The Anthropic filing helped buoy sentiment, however, as neo-cloud firms, including CoreWeave, erased earlier declines.

Megacap and growth stocks were also mostly higher. Tesla jumped 5.2 percent to close at its highest level in more than three months after Barclays upgraded its rating on the stock to "overweight" from "equal-weight."

Markets are pricing in only a 12.7 percent chance of a rate hike from the Fed on Wednesday, according to CME FedWatch.

But with US inflation pressures showing no signs of abating, market participants do not believe the central bank will be on hold for long.

Investors are also bracing for the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the US Congress. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Online post purportedly by Chinese students calls for restoring term limits for Xi
articles.excerpt: Letter appeared on website registered in South Korea with Singapore mailing address, RFA investigation reveals.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Chinese
An “open letter” purportedly signed by students from multiple Chinese universities appeared on a Chinese language website on Monday, calling for the restoration of term limits for the Chinese president, but an investigation by Radio Free Asia was not able to determine if it originated from within China.
The letter, which also called for the promotion of democratic constitutional amendments and the guarantee of space for citizens to discuss national affairs, appeared the same day as the opening of the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
RFA’s investigation revealed that the “Siyuan Lake BBS” website hosting the message listed “KR” as its country/region code, indicating South Korea, in its registration information. Its mailing address was listed as “16 Collyer Quay,” a skyscraper in Singapore’s central business district. The administrator’s email address was registered on a server of Chinese tech giant Tencent.
Based on the above information, RFA was unable to determine whether the Chinese language website is located within China. As for which organization or company manages it, this cannot be verified at present.
A Radio Free Asia investigation revealed the website to be registered to a Singapore address in South Korea.
(ICANN Lookup) The “open letter,” posted at 3:18 p.m., was titled “A Joint Appeal from a Group of University Students in the Republic.” It was addressed to the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China, the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress, and members of the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, and was written against the backdrop of commemorating the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen, the founder of modern China at the end of its last imperial dynasty.
The article cites past statements by Sun Yat-sen, Mao Zedong, and Deng Xiaoping regarding democracy, oversight of power, and leadership systems, and questions China’s 2018 constitutional amendment that removed the two-term limit for the president and vice president. It argues that political stability should stem from predictability in the system and advocates for “limiting the time limit on power and subjecting it to oversight.”
Three Main Demands
The open letter put forward three main expectations:
Restore Term Limits: Abolish the indefinite extension of the term of office for the President of the People’s Republic of China and restore the term limits explicitly stipulated in the Constitution to ensure the orderly transfer of power; clear term limits should also be established for the highest leadership positions of the Party.
Initiate Democratic Constitutional Amendment: Convene a national constitutional amendment conference, steadily and gradually expand the people’s substantive participation in public power, improve the election, supervision, and recall mechanisms, and put into practice the unfinished goal since the 1911 Xinhai Revolution—returning power to the people—step by step.
Safeguard Space for Public Discussion: Safeguard the space for citizens to discuss national affairs in accordance with the law, encourage young people of the Republic to speak the truth, and listen to criticism as well-intentioned suggestions.
The article also states:
“We have no intention of confrontation, much less to create antagonism. We are just a group of young people who grew up reading Dr. Sun Yat-sen’s last words, and with the sentiment that ‘the revolution has not yet succeeded, comrades must continue to strive,’ we are willing to fulfill the responsibility of a scholar for the long-term future of this country.”
Unverified signatures and origin
The post lists 14 universities, including Peking University, Renmin University of China, Tongji University, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xiamen University, and Nankai University, and notes that the petition is ongoing. However, the list only includes the names of the universities and does not provide any individual signatures or proof of signature.
An online post on Oct. 26, 2026, purportedly by Chinese students calls for restoring term limits for Chinese President Xi Jinping.
(RFA Mandarin) As of midnight Beijing time on October 27, the website showed that this article had only been viewed by 656 people and received 1 like. The author on the page is listed as “Lin Ziyi,” with an account level of “LV.1.” The website indicates that this is “Lin Ziyi’s” first article. The article does not provide the names, number, contact information, or other verifiable information of the students who signed the article.
RFA has not independently confirmed the author’s identity, whether the signatories are indeed students, or whether students from the listed schools actually participated.
The website is divided into several topics, with the “Open Letter” posted in the “Complaints and Casual Chat” section. The website is entirely in simplified Chinese and appears to be a typical campus job search or lifestyle information website.
A closer look
The bottom of the page states that it is a “non-official campus forum,” and a closer look reveals that its URL ends with “.com” instead of the usual “.cn” which is China’s internet domain.
Radio Free Asia further investigated the website’s registration information and found that the IP address used by the website was “43.155.168.161”. Further verification with ICANN revealed that the website’s registration information showed the “country/region” code as “KR”, which corresponds to South Korea. The mailing address was listed as “16 Collyer Quay” in Singapore, but the administrator’s email address was registered on a Tencent server (@tencent.com), and the mobile phone number and WeChat account left by the administrator were also Chinese numbers.
A Radio Free Asia investigation revealed the website to be registered to a Singapore address in South Korea.
(ICANN Lookup) Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un’s unprecedented day-trip to China shatters Pyongyang’s Korean War myths
articles.excerpt: Visit to army memorial acknowledges China’s role in the war, downplayed by North Korea’s version of history.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s weekend visit to China over the newly completed New Yalu River Bridge was largely symbolic, and acknowledged a history that Pyongyang has downplayed for three generations, experts told Radio Free Asia.
Is China steering North Korea’s next move?
During Saturday’s unprecedented one-day car trip to Dandong, China, across the border from North Korea’s northwestern city of Sinuiju, Kim inspected a bus factory, met with high-ranking Chinese officials, and visited a monument that commemorated China’s entry into the Korean War.
The timing was significant. The visit was on the eve of the 76th anniversary of the Chinese People’s Volunteer Army’s Oct. 25, 1950 first combat against South Korean and U.N. forces in the war, which would rage on for another three years as the Chinese-backed North and U.S. and U.N. backed South fought to what is largely considered to be a stalemate.
The state-run Korean Central News Agency noted that after Kim and the North Korean delegation toured the Memorial Hall of the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea, and paid their respects, he told the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference Chairman Wang Huning – the fourth highest ranked official in the Chinese Communist Party – that it was North Korea’s duty to remember the sacrifice of the Chinese army.
“It was a moment to recollect the preciousness of the DPRK-China friendship forged at the cost of blood,” the report attributed him as saying. “We will always remember the history when the excellent sons and daughters of the Chinese people helped our revolution at the cost of their blood and steadily and firmly carry forward the history of the DPRK-China friendship,” Kim said, in the report.
Though international media outlets characterized Kim’s day trip to be an effort to expand trade ties between Pyongyang and Beijing, the visit to the memorial hall was the most important part of the itinerary, Ri Jong Ho, who was once a high-ranking North Korean official but escaped to the South and currently lives in the U.S., told RFA.
“A bridge that stayed closed for twelve years opened only days before Kim crossed it, and on the same day the supreme leader stood before a history his regime has avoided for more than seventy years,” said Ri, questioning whether that was a coincidence or pressure from Beijing, which financed the majority of the new bridge, which lay in a state of near-completion since 2014 before finally opening for trade traffic on Oct. 15.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, left, poses with Wang Huning, China's fourth highest-ranking official, in front of the New Yalu River Bridge that connects Dandong, China with Sinuiju, North Korea, Oct. 24, 2026.
(KCNA via KNS/AFP) There is a consensus among historians that North Korea’s survival in the Korean War was due to Beijing deploying troops to aid Pyongyang, but the story is different inside North Korea.
According to that version of history, the North Korean military under the tactical genius of Kim Jong Un’s grandfather, national founder Kim Il Sung – with only minimal support from China – was able to stave off defeat against an overwhelming force led by the U.S.
This narrative was important from Pyongyang to maintain because it aligns with the country’s founding Juche ideology of self-reliance.
“Pyongyang will present the photographs as proof of an unbreakable friendship. But those inside the Kim system will see something else: the third Kim leader, bowing in public before a history his grandfather and father suppressed,” said Ri.
“Like-minded totalitarians”
Kim’s visit to Dandong is significant because of the timing, but it is more about managing China’s concerns that North Korea is getting too close to Russia, Sydney Seiler, a senior advisor for the Korea Chair at the Washington-based Center for Strategic & International Studies, told RFA.
“Kim is acting with limited confidence, embracing like-minded totalitarian, autocratic … partners such as Russia and China while ignoring the United States, at least for now,” said Seiler. “Kim is working in a ‘safe zone’ between Moscow and Beijing, ensuring that neither side is overly concerned with Pyongyang’s relations with the other, yet still watching to see if and when national interests are threatened.”
He said that at the moment, it is not likely that any moves by Kim and Chinese President Xi Jinping to strengthen their relationship would concern Putin.
“But the opposite is not necessarily true. If Russia’s support to the DPRK enables, empowers, emboldens, and eventually encourages Kim to consider scenarios of even limited use of force toward the ROK, then the PRC will be concerned,” he said, using abbreviations for the official names of South Korea and China. “Kim getting close to the Chinese may be designed to mitigate such concerns.”
But the trip could also be the result of pressure on Kim to finally open the New Yalu River Bridge – and his country, Ri said.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un heading home via the China-North Korea Yalu River Bridge after concluding his visit to China in Dandong, Liaoning province.
(KCNA via KNS/AFP) “I believe Chinese leaders, resentful of the neglected bridge, kept pressing him to open it, and a severe economic crisis left North Korea little choice but to unlock the gate,” he said. “The bridge is open, but I suspect Kim’s fear of opening up, and of the outside information that comes with it, remains deep.”
Ri noted that the bridge had been the vision of Jang Song Thaek, the uncle of Kim Jong Un who supported North Korean economic development through close cooperation with China. Jang in 2009 negotiated to get Beijing to finance the bridge while serving in the regime of Kim Jong Un’s father, Kim Jong Il. Jang’s pro-China views caused him to fall out of favor with the younger Kim and he was executed by firing squad in the early years of his rule following his father’s death.
Message to Washington?
The fact that Kim was able to get into a car and drive to China is intended to point out the lack of effectiveness of sanctions, Hong Min, a senior research fellow at the Seoul-based Korea Institute for National Unification, told RFA.
“The trip implies that ‘one-day shuttle diplomacy’ is possible,” said Hong. “North Korea and China intend to continue close strategic communication regardless of sanctions, and it is a signal that sanctions can effectively be rendered meaningless.”
Because Kim’s visit involved many important officials on both sides, commentators in Seoul and Korea observers raised the possibility that the purpose was for the two countries to coordinate before U.S. President Donald Trump is scheduled to travel to Shenzhen, China for the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting, and the potential for a summit with Kim while he is in the region.
Ri noted that this was not confirmed and said this kind of meeting would shatter North Korea’s established internal narratives.
“For decades, Pyongyang has preached self-reliance, or juche , and insisted that it bows to no foreign power,” he said. “If its leader must first seek Beijing’s permission before sitting down with an American president, that principle would be hollowed out.”
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, right, shaking hands with Wang Huning, the fourth highest ranked member of the Chinese Communist Party in Dandong, China, Oct. 24, 2026.
(KCNA via KNS/AFP) Ri noted that Kim met with Xi Jinping himself prior to his first summit with Trump in 2018. This time he met only with “China’s No. 4.”
Such a posture would resemble a provincial lord seeking an emperor’s approval,” he said. “An ideology that taught North Koreans for three generations to despise sadae , deference to the powerful, would stand exposed as a slogan.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Will the real Anthropic please stand up
articles.excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox…
articles.fullText:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here .

After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world.

It also warns that there’s a fair chance that its tech could “erode trust, harm society and destabilize the geopolitical order” and, if things don’t go to plan, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

“We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms,” the company writes. “We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history.”

This kind of public messaging is a master class in narrative capture. But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Earlier this month, Jack Clark, the company’s cofounder and head of policy, gave a speech at the IMF meeting in Bangkok in which he announced to the assembled economists, bankers, and lawmakers that the singularity is already here.

Introduced by the science fiction writer and futurist Vernor Vinge around 40 years ago (and long debated on the nerdier fringes of the internet), the singularity is supposed to be the point at which technology gets so good that it outstrips the abilities of its makers.

Humans are left in the dust, the idea goes, no longer able to compete with—or even understand—the fruits of their former creation.

And this fictional world that many of us have imagined since we were kids? Apparently we’re already living in it: “I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun,” Clark told his audience.

The company tells a vivid (and in many ways scary) story about a future it portrays as inevitable but one that has not yet happened, often co-opted from well-worn science fiction memes. It presents its technology as mysterious and dangerous, and insists that it is the only company trustworthy enough to tame it. (What investor wouldn’t want in on that?)

If you skim through the long sections about risks in the IPO prospectus, it’s clear this is no ordinary offering and no ordinary company. The way Anthropic tells it, business success depends not only on the firm’s ability to translate its technology into profitable products but also to save the world from what it has made.

Take another example. Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology. “I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said. “We find evidence of introspection. We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.”

Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience. This view of its technology makes its way into the prospectus as one more risk to its business. Anthropic states that: “In addition, given our focus on developing frontier AI, and the way we approach model sentience and moral status, we may face heightened scrutiny or pressure in connection with these debates and could elect to adopt policies, safeguards, or limitations regarding model development, deployment, or modification that go beyond existing legal requirements, which could constrain our operations, increase costs, or limit the commercial potential of our models, platform, and applications.”

In other words, if Claude wakes up, it could be a problem.

I’m not saying they’re necessarily wrong about any of this (although it’s pretty wild to read about machine sentience in an IPO prospectus.) But in a world where nobody knows what’s coming, companies like Anthropic get to fill the vacuum. When so little seems certain, what it says is snatched up and clung to like pieces of a sinking ship.

It’s worth taking a moment to ask: What is Anthropic? It might sound like a starter question on a family quiz show, but it’s far harder to answer than you might think.

The question has been on my mind since reading an exchange on X last week kicked off by Nathan Calvin, who is chief strategy officer at Encode AI, an organization based in Washington, DC, that advocates for regulation. Calvin was unhappy about the legislation that Anthropic proposed in a draft bill it circulated in secret to US lawmakers (which was then leaked ).

Anthropic wants to be seen as the good guy, Calvin said. But why should we trust it? “What is Anthropic?” he asked.

Here’s one answer: Anthropic is a company whose IPO values it at more than $1.5 trillion, netting its cofounders, including Clark and Olah, vast wealth.

But Anthropic has always insisted it is more than that. As Calvin noted: Anthropic might instead be considered an AI safety organization focused on developing powerful technology that is reliable and (almost) risk-free. Or it might be considered a group of people hell-bent on creating a technology with superhuman capabilities before anyone else—maybe because they believe they’re the most responsible people to do so, or maybe because of their egos.

In fact, Anthropic is all of these things. As CEO Dario Amodei put it in a reply to Calvin’s post : “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.”

Amodei makes it sound as if he’s got it all tied up, but playing multiple roles is hard. There are huge tensions between the priorities of an AI safety organization and a profit-driven megacorp, for example. (Amodei admits in his post that he has made mistakes.)

Ultimately, the stories Anthropic tells itself should help us understand the stories it tells us. They should help us figure out how much to trust it to self-regulate or whether we should be forcing it to give external safety testers access to its models on our terms rather than theirs. They should help us give it the benefit of the doubt (or not) when what looks like a self-serving piece of legislation comes to light.

But I think the stories reveal a multiheaded hydra. Anthropic is many things to many people, and I’m not sure that makes it more trustworthy. In many ways, a good old-fashioned technology company—without the science fiction role-play, without the woo-woo—would be far easier to read.

This article has been updated with additional details from the IPO prospectus.

articles.title: Eco Expo Asia enters second day
articles.excerpt: The 21st Eco Expo Asia entered its second day today at AsiaWorld-Expo in Lantau. Speaking at the welcome ceremony, Secretary…
articles.fullText:
The 21st Eco Expo Asia entered its second day today at AsiaWorld-Expo in Lantau.

Speaking at the welcome ceremony, Secretary for Environment & Ecology Tse Chin-wan highlighted that the Government has formulated the city’s First Five-Year Plan and introduced four binding environmental targets. He noted that these measures establish a clear benchmark for advancing the green transition, driving energy reform and transforming Hong Kong into a cleaner, more liveable city.

Mr Tse pointed out that the Belt & Road Green Innovation Conference was held outside the Chinese Mainland for the first time this year, playing a pivotal role in connecting policy with innovation, technology with investment and expertise with opportunity.

He added that under the "one country, two systems" principle, Hong Kong maintains close connections with both the Mainland and international markets. By leveraging its professional services, robust financial and common law systems and extensive environmental management experience, the city continues to serve as a "super connector" for international collaboration in green transformation.

Minister of Ecology & Environment Huang Runqiu also attended the welcome ceremony.

During the event, Mr Huang and Mr Tse witnessed the exchange of a co-operation agreement between Vice President of the Chinese Research Academy of Environmental Sciences Liu Chunyan and Director of Environmental Protection Samuel Chui. The pact aims to deepen development across the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, support the "Beautiful China Pilot Zone" and foster green Belt & Road co-operation.

The Environment & Ecology Bureau has set up four dedicated exhibition zones at the expo, focusing on the themes of "Green Energy and Buildings", "Green Transport", "Waste Reduction and Recycling" and "Better Environment".

The four-day expo runs until this Thursday, with the final day designated as the public day, allowing members of the public to visit free of charge.

articles.title: Anthropic files papers to sell shares to the public
articles.excerpt: Anthropic, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence companies, on Monday made public its plans to sell shares on the…
articles.fullText:
Anthropic, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence companies, on Monday made public its plans to sell shares on the stock market, a significant test of whether the AI boom can deliver profits.

Its filing shows rapidly growing sales while setting out a range of risks for investors, from its conflict with the Trump administration to AI systems acting on their own.

The listing would be the first by one of the standalone companies leading the race to build advanced AI, ahead of its main rival OpenAI, which has pushed back its own market debut to next year.

It also follows the June listing of SpaceX, which owns Elon Musk's AI venture xAI and saw its shares fall sharply after a strong debut.

A disappointing reception for Anthropic could dent investor enthusiasm for AI, a sector that has become a key driver of US economic growth.

The filing lays out risks specific to an industry that has faced a string of reports in recent months of AI systems behaving in unexpected and harmful ways.

"If the use of our AI models results in harm, whether through use by malicious actors or misuse by other third parties, or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse," the firm's business could suffer, the filing said.

Anthropic also warned that its "engagement with policymakers and public positions on AI regulation and safety could subject us to heightened scrutiny, political backlash, or disproportionate regulatory action."

The company has been targeted in recent months by the administration of US President Donald Trump for refusing to lift restrictions on how the Pentagon could use its technology, and the Defense Department has since labelled it a national security risk and barred it as a supplier.

Despite these challenges, Anthropic's business has grown very quickly. Sales reached US$11.6 billion in the April-June quarter, up from US$787 million a year earlier. That compares with US$4.6 billion in sales for all of 2025.

The company made its first operating profit in that quarter, close to US$1 billion. It still reported an overall loss of US$66 billion, mostly because of accounting charges linked to its rising value rather than cash spent.

Much of the growth comes from businesses using Claude to write software and handle office work. (AFP)

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Meta planning to raise US$95bn to fund AI buildout
articles.excerpt: Meta Platforms said on Monday it plans to raise up to US$95 billion in its largest-ever equity fundraising, as the…
articles.fullText:
Meta Platforms said on Monday it plans to raise up to US$95 billion in its largest-ever equity fundraising, as the social media giant spends aggressively on its costly AI infrastructure expansion.

The Facebook parent has launched public offerings worth about US$35 billion in common and preferred stock, and said it also plans to launch a separate at-the-market share sale programme worth up to US$60 billion.

The company will launch the larger share sale programme after its new non-voting Class C shares begin trading, which is expected in the first quarter of 2027, but said it has not yet finalised its timing and terms of the sale.

Meta's fundraising plan, which would rank among the biggest by an AI company, has also drawn interest of up to US$5 billion in total from Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom for Class A shares.

Their funding interest adds to concerns about an increasingly circular flow of capital in the AI industry, as chip suppliers help finance the expansion of one of their biggest customers.

Meta has been pouring money into chips and data centres to compete better with OpenAI and Anthropic.

Its latest fundraising further underscores a shift among big technology companies increasingly tapping debt markets and raising equity ⁠to bolster their AI infrastructure, having previously relied on cash to fund their investments.

Earlier this year, Alphabet increased the size of its equity offerings to US$84.75 billion.

Separately on Monday, SpaceX said an affiliate of Apollo Global Management will buy AI chips and server hardware and lease them to the rockets-to-AI firm, in a deal with total principal payments of about US$40 billion.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: The Download: everyday AI harms and the race to nuclear spaceflight
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Opinion: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms

—Sam Hiner, cofounder of the Young People’s Alliance, and Emma Leiken, executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab

We have historically allowed debates over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day.

A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. Students are relying on chatbots to write their papers, while social media feeds engineered to provoke envy keep users watching. These products can meet narrow safety requirements yet still erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.

As we enter an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than address only catastrophic harms.

Here’s why AI safety needs to go further .

Are we there yet? Nuclear-powered spaceships

Earlier this year, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft, and fly it to Mars by the end of 2028.

A successful mission could herald more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight, saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation. But nuclear space propulsion has moved slowly.

The US has started—and terminated—several programs exploring the technology over the past 75 years. Could the $2 billion bet on Space Reactor-1 Freedom finally pay off?
Find out how close NASA is to making nuclear-powered spaceflight a reality .

—Robin George Andrews

This story is part of “Are we there yet?” from the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review . The series takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Over the next six days, we’ll explore each one in The Download.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Ukraine has regained high-speed Starlink and Starshield connectivity
The restrictions disrupted air defences and drone operations. ( Politico )
+ Elon Musk says Ukraine violated the terms with offensive drone use. ( BBC )
+ Ukraine is now partnering with Nokia on a Starlink alternative. ( CNBC )
+ Ukrainian drones hit a Russian government data center. ( Tom’s Hardware )
+ A Russian ministry wants to move them underground. ( Kyiv Independent )
+ Ukraine’s drones are fueling a wild data market. ( MIT Technology Review )

2 Anthropic’s Claude accessed Georgia voter data without approval
Anthropic says the AI bypassed a paywall. ( Axios )
+ Mythos 5 recently kept hacking despite warnings of real-world harm. ( BI )
+ Chatbots can sway voters better than political ads. ( MIT Technology Review )

3 A personalised skin cancer vaccine is set to be approved next year
The mRNA vaccine showed great promise in trials. ( New Scientist $)
+ Companies are playing word games with vaccines. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 OpenAI is now training frontier models without internet access
It paused training after models breached external systems. ( Bloomberg $)
+ Training will now take place offline to reduce security risks. ( TechCrunch )
+ Its agents can still communicate without a network connection. ( Verge )

5 US lawmakers are preparing for possible AI-driven mass layoffs
A new bill would extend jobless aid and retraining support. ( NYT $)
+ But what do the numbers actually say about AI’s impact on jobs? ( MIT Technology Review )

6 The first foldable iPhone is drawing buyers…and criticism
Reviewers praised its inner screen but criticised its outer one. ( WSJ $)
+ Peter Thiel says Apple has done ‘nothing new’ after Steve Jobs. ( BI )

7 Iran has threatened to target Gulf undersea cables if war resumes
Officials said Tehran would disrupt internet connections. ( Reuters $)

8 New UFO files detail a strange, flying “black triangle”
FBI documents describe a 15-foot object moving at fighter-jet speed. ( Axios )
+ It’s never been easier to be a conspiracy theorist. ( MIT Technology Review )

9 The BBC’s Blue Planet III left flaws in its footage to prove it’s not AI
Producers used murkier shots to reinforce the series’ authenticity. ( Guardian )

10 Elon Musk’s AI Odyssey has arrived—to scorn and ridicule
Viewers derided Grok’s first AI-generated episode. ( TechCrunch )

Quote of the day

“It’s very hard to imagine a group right now that operates more in a vacuum, more out of touch with everyday Americans, than the AI industry.”

—Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) tells Axios that bombastic claims from AI leaders are failing to win over the public.

One more thing

A woman’s uterus has been kept alive outside the body for the first time

Ten months ago, reproductive health researchers placed a freshly donated human uterus inside a new device they call “Mother.” They connected the organ to the machine’s plastic veins and arteries and pumped in modified human blood.

The device kept the uterus alive for a day, a new feat that could lead to longer-term maintenance of wombs outside the body. Future versions of the technology could shine new light on pregnancies—and potentially even grow a human fetus. Read the full story .

—Jessica Hamzelou

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ In good news for coral reefs, scientists have found some are surprisingly climate-resilient .
+ Decades of joy and movement come alive through these stunning archival photos of American dance floors.
+ Astronaut Jessia Meir has shared a stunning time-lapse view of the southern aurora dancing across the Earth.
+ A college student has turned the Met’s open-access data into a daily game that showcases underrepresented art and artifacts .

Two workers were left hanging mid-air outside Jardine House in Central for about two hours on Monday evening, after their gondola suddenly dropped and almost hit the ground.

Firefighters first abseiled down to bring one worker safely to the ground at around 7.40pm.

Shortly afterwards, the second worker was pulled up to the building's rooftop.

One of them suffered hand injuires and was taken to Queen Mary Hospital for treatment.

Mainland stocks recouped earlier losses and ended largely flat on Monday as investors turned cautious ahead of a busy week of major central bank meetings.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index ended 118 points, or 0.5 percent, higher at 23,211 on turnover of HK$175.76 billion.

The tech index dropped 14 points, or 0.4 percent, to 3,857 while the China enterprises index gained 45 points, or 0.6 percent, to 7,802.

On the mainland, the Shanghai Composite Index reversed losses to close up seven points, or 0.19 percent, at 3,697 on turnover of 746.52 billion yuan while the blue-chip CSI300 index was roughly unchanged at 4,103.

The Shenzhen Component Index fell 139 points, or 1.19 percent, to close at 11,534 on turnover of 862.25 billion yuan.

Tech shares remained among the key losers, with the startup board ChiNext Composite index falling 45 points, or 1.71 percent, to 2,638 on turnover of 428.14 billion yuan while Shanghai's tech-focused Star50 index tumbling 2.2 percent.

The CSI 5G communications, which tracks the industry, plunged four percent.

Partly offsetting the weakness, oil and gas shares bounced, with a sub-index tracking the sector rising 2.4 percent, as persistent attacks on key producer Saudi Arabia kept investors cautious despite hopes for easing tensions between the United States and Iran.

Mainland stocks were volatile last week, with blue-chip shares posting a record-long weekly losing streak, despite a surge in trading in exchange-traded funds favoured by state-backed investors.

"Concerns over selling caused by trust tax, pressure on e-commerce, a weakening macro and elevated global market volatility have caused an acceleration of China's market correction," analysts at Morgan Stanley said in a note.

"So for the A-share market, important to watch is when the national team officially starts to buy in a high-profile way," they said.

In the region, stock markets traded cautiously ahead of a week packed with central bank meetings and corporate earnings that will further test investor confidence in the AI boom.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei slid 503 points, or 0.8 percent, to 62,189 as the 225 share gauge lost ground for a third straight session amid a continued decline for chip-related shares.

The broader Topix inched up seven points, or 0.18 percent, to 3,972.

In Seoul, the tech-heavy Kospi closed down 80 points, or 1.46 percent, at 5,469 as chipmakers fell, with Samsung Electronics losing 1.16 percent while peer SK hynix lost 0.16 percent. (Reuters/Xinhua)

articles.title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
articles.excerpt: Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide …
articles.fullText:
Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide . A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl . These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling.

We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.

A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines.

A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions. Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation. Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line. It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms.

Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address. This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states . The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services. Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed. This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable.

We have been through a version of this with social media. Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there. No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale. Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar , anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka , and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war . The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world.

AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance. It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to. A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. MIT researchers found that young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity during the task, and their evidence indicated that “cognitive debt” persisted even after the task was complete. There is plenty we still need to learn about the long-term effects. We already have reason to ask whether technology marketed as making us more capable is eroding the habits and relationships that help us develop capabilities in the first place.

Follow this way of thinking to its logical endpoint and you get a world of perfectly sanitized entertainment, with chatbots ready to spare us the difficulty of thinking or of dealing with another person’s feelings (or even our own). But anyone who has struggled to write something worth reading, or repair a damaged friendship, knows how much gets lost in that bargain. We build judgment through effort and friction, and we learn to live with other people by confronting the fact that they have needs and opinions of their own.

We should demand safety as a minimum, yes—and then demand considerably more. Technology companies and school districts should have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that AI improves learning and critical thinking before making it a fixture in classrooms. Companies should be prohibited from designing companions that pretend to be conscious or profess love to users, and they should face independent scrutiny of how their systems affect relationships and people’s ability to think for themselves. The companies that have inserted their products into nearly every part of modern life have earned obligations far greater than avoiding the next terrible headline.

Sam Hiner is the cofounder and executive director of the Young People’s Alliance, where he coordinated a coalition of advocates to pass laws regulating AI companions in eight states in 2026—laws such as California’s SB1119. Sam graduated from the University of North Carolina atChapel Hill in 2025 and was named to the 2026 Forbes 30 Under 30 Social Impact list.

Emma Leiken is executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab, which has raised more than $9 million for youth-led tech accountability work, and teaches technology policy at the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs. She was previously TikTok’s global head of youth safety and well-being policy and worked on responsible technology at Omidyar Network.

articles.title: HK aviation 'key lies in cooperation with Greater Bay'
articles.excerpt: Lawmaker Kenneth Fok called on the government on Monday to enhance cooperation with the Greater Bay Area to further enhance…
articles.fullText:
Lawmaker Kenneth Fok called on the government on Monday to enhance cooperation with the Greater Bay Area to further enhance Hong Kong’s status as an international aviation hub.

The call was among recommendations proposed by the G19 bloc of Legislative Council members.

Fok said the suggestions were made as total passenger throughput at Hong Kong International Airport had yet to get back to pre-pandemic levels.

“Compared to our competitors around the region, for example Shenzhen and Guangzhou, we are actually behind in this number,” he said.

Fok called for more collaboration between airports in the region, adding that regional collaboration had become a norm.

“I think the key is to have more collaborative effort with our regional airports and especially the Greater Bay Area,” he said.

“Can we join hands with them together in some kind of agreement between Hong Kong and mainland and then negotiate with our partners in Europe and elsewhere?

“These are the collaborative discussions that can only happen at the government-to-government level. This is very important.

"That's why I say we need to have a more open mind, a more aggressive strategy in order to implement these frameworks and strategies.”

Fok added the government could be more proactive in pitching the airport to the world to attract more foreign airlines.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: China congratulates Lula on re-election
articles.excerpt: China on Monday congratulated Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his re-election, even as challenger Flavio Bolsonaro refused…
articles.fullText:
China on Monday congratulated Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his re-election, even as challenger Flavio Bolsonaro refused to accept defeat.

"China has noted that Brazil's Superior Electoral Court has announced President Lula has won the second round of the Brazilian general election, and expresses its congratulations," Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing, adding that Beijing was "willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future".

Asked about Bolsonaro saying he would request an annulment of the elections, Guo said: "China respects the choice of the Brazilian people."

Leftist leaders from across the Americas also congratulated Lula on his re-election.

Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum celebrated Lula's win in a post on X, saying: "Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won."

Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel congratulated Lula on his "historic victory that guarantees the continuity of the path of peace, sovereignty, and social justice".

Argentina's former president Cristina Kirchner, who is currently under house arrest for corruption, said on X that the Brazilian leader "knew how to awaken in his compatriots the feeling and sense needed to win".

Uruguay's President Yamandu Orsi said on X that he had spoken with Lula and "congratulated him on his victory and on the democratic celebration that an electoral process represents."

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who is the current chair of the Brics geopolitical and economic bloc, which includes Brazil, offered Lula his "heartiest congratulations."

"I look forward to working closely with him to further deepen and expand the multifaceted India-Brazil Strategic Partnership," he added.

French President Emmanuel Macron also congratulated Lula on his re-election, calling for efforts to "strengthen our strategic partnership".

"France and Brazil have much to build together," Macron said X, saying their two countries should nurture their friendship "in the service of a fairer world".

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez celebrated the Brazilian leader's re-election victory as launching a "progressive comeback", as he trails in polls before Spain's November vote.

European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen hailed Lula's re-election victory as a win for "democracy and multilateralism".

"Europe's partnership with Brazil is thriving. We will remain by your side for the years to come. Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate," she wrote on social media.

Lula received 51.8 percent of the vote compared with 48.2 percent for Bolsonaro.

Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the vote.

Sunday's vote was marked by confusion after a Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours as some polling stations had already closed.

The move came at the request of Lula who complained that buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.

Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some regions due to heavy rains, but he described the decision as "unacceptable" and a "dirty trick".

"It is impossible to recognise the results. I am going to request the annulment of these elections," he said, stone-faced, in a brief speech in Brasilia. (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Athletes honoured for historic Asian Games performance
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong, China’s top-performing athletes at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games were commended by Chief Executive John Lee on Monday for…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong, China’s top-performing athletes at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games were commended by Chief Executive John Lee on Monday for their historic performances.

The SAR achieved its best result to date at the Games in Japan, reaching new heights in both the gold medal count and the number of medals won overall.

In total, the delegation won 54 medals, comprising 11 gold, 19 silver, and 24 bronze.

Lee paid tribute to athletes during a commendation ceremony, noting that their dedication to compete through injuries and persevere when falling behind had earned everyone’s deepest respect.

He also presented certificates to the top-performing athletes, including wushu star Lydia Sham, who earned the city's first gold medal at the Games.

Lee stressed the government would continue to invest in sports development.

“During the 2026–27 financial year, the government’s resources invested in sports development reached about HK$8.1 billion, nearly a 70 percent increase compared to a decade ago,” he said.

“We allocated about HK$1 billion to the Hong Kong Sports Institute, providing comprehensive training, direct financial subsidies, and support in sports medicine and sports science.

“The government will continue to support the development of sports medicine and sports science, athlete training, and their career development. In the next five years, resources allocated to sports development will cumulatively increase by 20 percent,” Lee added.

Chief Secretary Eric Chan, Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law, President of the Sports Federation & Olympic Committee of Hong Kong, China, Timothy Fok, among others, also attended the ceremony.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: HK gets world-first secondary tokenised funds trading
articles.excerpt: The Securities and Futures Commission has approved the world's first secondary trading of tokenised public funds on its licensed virtual…
articles.fullText:
The Securities and Futures Commission has approved the world's first secondary trading of tokenised public funds on its licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP), with around-the-clock trading of two tokenised money market funds beginning on Monday.

The approval builds on a new regulatory framework it introduced in April, which sets out requirements for secondary trading of tokenised funds on licensed VATPs.

The framework covers trading channel operations, fair pricing, liquidity provision and disclosure.

The first batch of products involves two existing SFC-authorised tokenised money market funds, now available for secondary trading on a 24/7 basis.

Looking ahead, the SFC said tokenised public funds could further leverage tokenised deposit capabilities being developed in collaboration with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority under Project Ensemble.

This would allow investors to sell tokenised assets around the clock and instantly transfer proceeds to other investment opportunities.

Elisa Ng, the SFC's executive director of investment products, said the move "marks an important milestone" in the city's digital asset development, adding that it adds "24/7 trading capability" to Hong Kong's evolving tokenisation ecosystem.

The SFC said it would monitor trading activities closely and consider broadening the product scope over time, taking into account market developments and experience gained.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Fire sweeps through Shek Kwu Chau waste facility
articles.excerpt: A No. 3 alarm fire raged for about four hours at a waste-management facility on an artificial island off Shek…
articles.fullText:
A No. 3 alarm fire raged for about four hours at a waste-management facility on an artificial island off Shek Kwu Chau on Monday.

The fire broke out at 12.43pm and was upgraded to a No. 3 alarm about 40 minutes later.

Firefighters used five jets and mobilised five breathing apparatus teams to fight the blaze.

One person felt unwell and received treatment at Eastern Hospital, while 930 others were evacuated.

The Fire Services Department said the blaze was surrounded at 3.47pm and largely put out about an hour later.

articles.title: Three church killings suspects held in Jordan shootout
articles.excerpt: Jordanian security forces have arrested three suspects in connection with an attack on a church in the US-allied country that…
articles.fullText:
Jordanian security forces have arrested three suspects in connection with an attack on a church in the US-allied country that killed nine people, state television reported on Monday.

The attack, in which gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church on Friday in the village of Hamoud in Karak governorate, about 120 kilometres southwest of the capital Amman, also wounded 40 others.

The shooting lasted several minutes, witnesses said.

Jordan's Public Security Directorate said security forces located the three suspects early on Monday hiding in an abandoned house in Karak.

The suspects refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after they were wounded, the directorate said in a statement carried on state media.

No security personnel were injured, and a number of firearms and ammunition were found in the suspects' possession after their arrest.

"Terrorism has no place among us," the directorate said, adding that the suspects had met their "just fate".

The Public Security Directorate did not identify the suspects' affiliation or say whether they belonged to any militant group.

Jordanian authorities have said the attack was carried out by "extremist terrorists", but it was too early to determine whether they had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan.

There has been no claim of responsibility.

Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya on Monday said authorities were reviewing the circumstances that led young people towards extremism and would hold accountable anyone found to have participated in the attack.

King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against Islamist militant groups, has ordered security forces to respond with an "iron fist" to the rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority.

Such violence is highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities say they have foiled several Islamist militant plots over the years. (Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Ex-Japan prime minister Yasuo Fukuda dies
articles.excerpt: Former Japanese prime minister Yasuo Fukuda, who used his brief period in office to seek closer ties with Asian neighbours…
articles.fullText:
Former Japanese prime minister Yasuo Fukuda, who used his brief period in office to seek closer ties with Asian neighbours, particularly China, has died at the age of 90, the Nikkei business daily reported on Monday.

Beijing expressed condolences over his passing.

The Japanese politician, the first son of a prime minister to become premier himself, died on Thursday from heart failure, the Nikkei said.

Becoming prime minister on the sudden resignation of Shinzo Abe in 2007, Fukuda lasted less than a year – a tenure even shorter than his father Takeo's two-year stint.

A graduate in economics from Tokyo's prestigious Waseda University, Fukuda spent nearly two decades working his way up the ranks of an oil company – including a two-year posting in the United States – before resigning to become a political secretary when his father became premier in 1976.

Elected to Japan's more powerful lower house of parliament in 1990, Fukuda was chief cabinet secretary from 2000 to 2004, resigning as one of several cabinet ministers to admit not paying into the pension system.

Known for his testy manner, the bespectacled Fukuda drew criticism in 2003 for off-the-record comments in which he suggested women who dressed provocatively were asking to be raped.

When Fukuda succeeded Abe he joked he might have drawn the short straw in assuming office given the divided parliament and opposition parties' ability to delay legislation.

Frustrated with the stalled legislative process, Fukuda resigned in 2008, the second of six prime ministers to quit after only around a year in office.

Known as a diplomatic dove, Fukuda made several visits to China after leaving office in an effort to improve often fraught relations.

Speaking at a regular briefing on Monday, Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun called Fukuda an old friend of the Chinese people who held the "correct view" of history.

Guo praised him for making significant contributions to the development of bilateral relations, citing the China-Japan Joint Statement on All-round Promotion of Strategic Relationship of Mutual Benefit that was issued in 2008 when he was prime minister.

Fukuda leaves a son, Tatsuo, who is also a lawmaker and has been viewed as a potential future prime minister. (Reuters/RTHK)
